Three times he says “this Moses,” “this man,” “this man” (7:35, 37, 38), like someone in court pointing again and again at the same person: this is he, the very one you say I blaspheme. Then he asks: how did your fathers treat him? The answer is in verse 39: “Our fathers would not be obedient, but rejected him, and in their hearts turned back to Egypt.” While Moses was still on the mountain receiving God’s word, the people below were already making a calf.
I. “God will raise up for you a prophet like me”—Moses Himself Points to Another
Verse 37: Stephen quotes Deuteronomy 18:15: God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me.

This is a very clever and very honest step in the defense. The council had accused him: “Jesus will change the customs that Moses delivered to us.” Stephen says: Moses himself said that another would come, and you must listen to him. Moses is not the end; he pointed to the end with his own mouth. So those who truly honor Moses will listen to the prophet “like Moses,” and those who reject that prophet are the ones who truly despise Moses.

“Like me”—like Moses, raised up from among the brothers, rejected by the brothers, yet appointed by God as deliverer. Peter already used this verse in chapter three (Acts 3:22), and no one in the council could fail to understand whom he meant.
• Scripture is my standard, and Scripture points to Jesus: if you read Moses and do not find Christ, you have not understood Moses.
• A faithful servant points to the Lord, not to himself: one of Moses’ greatest services was to say, “Not me, but the One who is coming.”
II. “He received living oracles to give to us”—Moses Was a Messenger
Verse 38 says Moses was in the assembly in the wilderness, on Mount Sinai, with the angel who spoke to him and with our fathers, and “received living oracles to give to us.”

“Living oracles” in the original is “living words”—not dead regulations, but the living speech of God. Moses stood between two sides: on one side the God who spoke to him, on the other the people waiting to hear. His work was to “receive” and then “give.” Not one sentence was his own; all of it was received.

This is just what Jesus was like—“The words that I say to you, I do not speak from myself” (John 14:10). A messenger may not add or subtract. The council kept the letter of the law but treated the law as their own inheritance, forgetting that it was “living,” that God is still speaking.
• Receive in order to give: if I have received nothing from God today, I have nothing to give to others.
• The word is living: the law is not a museum relic but what God is still saying; if reading Scripture does not let me hear what God is saying now, it is only reading letters.
III. “Would not be obedient, but rejected him, and in their hearts turned back to Egypt”—In the Wilderness in Body, in Egypt at Heart

Verses 39–40: our fathers “would not be obedient, but rejected him.” This is the third “rejection” in the sermon: Joseph sold, Moses pushed away, and now Moses rejected a second time—this time not in Egypt, but in the wilderness, after leaving Egypt, just past the Red Sea, with the miracles still warm.

“In their hearts turned back to Egypt” is an extremely accurate diagnosis. Their feet had left Egypt, but their hearts had not. When Moses had been on the mountain forty days, they told Aaron: “Make us gods which will go before us; for as for this Moses, who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we don’t know what has become of him.” Notice what they call Moses: “this Moses”—contemptuous, distant, replaceable at any time.

Someone has emigrated to a new country for many years, yet his watch is still set to the old country’s time, and the first thing he does each morning is read the news from home. The body has moved; the heart has not. Believers can be like this: the body in church, but the desires, standards and sense of security of the heart all still in “Egypt.” Changing from a human viewpoint to God’s viewpoint, from worldly to God’s, is a change of heart, not only of feet.
• Leaving Egypt is once, turning back in heart is any moment: ask daily, to which time zone is my heart set today?
• Note what you call those God sends: “this Moses” or “the Moses God sent”—the way you name them hides the direction of your heart.
IV. “Rejoiced in the works of their hands”—Worshiping What You Made Is Worshiping Yourself
Verse 41: they made a calf, brought a sacrifice to the idol, and “rejoiced in the works of their hands.”

This line is the deepest cut in the passage. What is the essence of idolatry? Not worshiping an ox but worshiping “the works of their hands.” A person makes a god and then bows down to it—which is bowing down to his own hands. What that god says and wants is entirely decided by the one who made it; so idolatry from beginning to end is man being king.

What Moses brought down was God’s word, which must be obeyed; the calf was man’s work, which could be managed. The fathers chose the latter, because then they were still lord. Today’s calf need not be gold; it may be a faith one has designed, a way of serving one approves, a church that feels comfortable—as long as it is “the work of my hands,” as long as I am still the one who decides before it, it is a calf.
• The mark of an idol: it never asks you to deny yourself; it only asks you to rejoice.
• Check what you rejoice in: God’s works or the works of your own hands? The former makes people humble, the latter makes them proud.
V. “But God turned and gave them up”—The Most Terrible Judgment Is Being Given Over

Verses 42–43: “But God turned and gave them up to serve the army of the sky.” Then Stephen quotes Amos 5: House of Israel, did you offer to me sacrifices forty years in the wilderness? You took up the tabernacle of Moloch and the star of the god Rephan. Therefore I will carry you away beyond Babylon.

“Gave them up” is the most terrible phrase in the Bible. God does not storm; He lets go—if you want to worship that, go and worship it. Romans 1 says three times that “God gave them up” (Rom. 1:24, 26, 28), all with the same meaning: when people insist on being king themselves, God lets them be king and taste the consequences.

Stephen’s quotation of Amos runs deep. Those “tabernacles” were tabernacles of foreign gods; in the next section he will speak of the “tabernacle of the testimony” God commanded Moses to make. Israel carried two tabernacles all along the way: one God’s, one their own making. The council thought the temple was their protection; Stephen says: your fathers carried images of their own making into the Promised Land, and the result was exile beyond Babylon.
• God’s silence is not consent: when He “turns away,” people often still feel everything is going well.
• Two tabernacles cannot be carried together: if the heart still carries a god of its own making, the temple outside cannot save you.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Worshiping the Work of Your Hands Is Being Your Own King
The center of this passage is verse 41: “rejoiced in the works of their hands.”

The old self, with its life of self, always makes itself a calf—not necessarily denying God, only making Him into a shape it can control: He should bless according to my expectations, approve my way of serving, stand on my side. Such a “god” is in the end made by one’s own hands, and worshiping him is worshiping oneself. And once a person worships the work of his own hands, he can no longer listen to those God sends—Moses on the mountain, the calf below; the two cannot both be king.

Letting Jesus be King is taking “the work of my hands” down from the throne. True oracles are received, not manufactured; true service is obeying the prophet God sent, not dancing around what we have made. Change the way of thinking and the life changes—from rejoicing in our own works to rejoicing in God’s works. Once that step is taken, the heart has moved out of Egypt.
a: Read Moses and Find Christ
Each time you read the Old Testament, ask: how does this point to Jesus?
Receive First, Then Pass On
If you haven’t heard anything from God today, don’t hurry to tell people anything.
Reset the Heart’s Time Zone
Is your security, your standard, your longing set to Egypt or to God today?
Find Your Calf
Which thing is “the work of your hands,” that you rejoice in and that you control?
Fear God’s Giving Over
When everything goes smoothly yet God seems to have stopped speaking, turn back and examine yourself.
q: “Rejoiced in the works of their hands.” In your faith life, is there something you made yourself, that you decide, that makes you rejoice yet never asks you to deny yourself? Could that be your calf?

The fathers called the one God sent “this Moses.” Have you used the tone of “that so-and-so” in your heart toward someone God sent to speak to you? Where does that tone show your heart is facing right now?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Moses did not point to himself but to the prophet who was to come; he did not speak his own words but passed on Your living oracles. Thank You for showing us that those You send are rejected all along the way, yet You speak faithfully all along, and even when our fathers’ hearts turned back to Egypt, Your word did not stop.
Lord, we confess that our feet often leave Egypt while our hearts remain there; we also often make the calf of our own hands, turning You into a shape we can control, rejoicing in our own work and unable to listen to those You send. Remove the “self” within us that wants to be king, take the work of our hands down from the throne, and let You sit there. Keep us from falling into being “given over,” and when You seem not to speak, make us watchful and turn us back. May we carry only Your tabernacle all our lives, and not images of our own making. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: “Our fathers had the tabernacle of the testimony in the wilderness, even as he who spoke to Moses commanded him to make it according to the pattern that he had seen;
which also our fathers, in their turn, brought in with Joshua when they entered into the possession of the nations, whom God drove out before the face of our fathers, to the days of David,
who found favor in the sight of God, and asked to find a habitation for the God of Jacob.
But Solomon built him a house.
However, the Most High doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands, as the prophet says,
‘heaven is my throne, and the earth a footstool for my feet. What kind of house will you build me?’ says the Lord. ‘Or what is the place of my rest?
Didn’t my hand make all these things?’
b: In the last devotion, Stephen spoke of the fathers making a calf in the wilderness, “rejoicing in the works of their hands,” and quoted Amos saying they carried the tabernacle of Moloch all along the way, and were carried away beyond Babylon.

Today he speaks of another tabernacle—“the tabernacle of the testimony,” the one God commanded Moses to make. From this tabernacle he moves to David, then to Solomon’s temple, and finally stops at a word of Isaiah: Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what kind of house will you build me? This is the summit of the first main theme of the whole sermon. The council had accused him of speaking against the holy place, and Stephen answers from Scripture: It is not I who defile the holy place; it is you who have made the holy place into God.
I. “According to the pattern that he had seen”—What God Gave Was a Tabernacle That Moves

Verse 44 says our fathers had “the tabernacle of the testimony” in the wilderness, because inside were the two tablets with the Ten Commandments, the witness of the covenant between God and man. This tabernacle was made “as he who spoke to Moses commanded him to make it according to the pattern that he had seen”—the pattern was given by God on the mountain, not thought up by man.

The calf of the last devotion was “the work of their hands”; the tabernacle of this devotion was made “according to the pattern that he had seen.” The difference between them is not the material but the source: one was designed by man for God, the other designed by God for man.

And what God designed was a tabernacle—a tent of cloth and poles, one that could be taken down, carried, and move along with the people. God wanted to dwell among His people, yet He chose a way that could move at any time. This itself is a message: He does not want to be fixed in one place.
• Service must follow God’s pattern: not how I want to worship God, but how God says He wants to be worshiped.
• God chose a tent: He would rather dwell in a tent of cloth, traveling with His people, than in a house of stone, apart from them.
II. “They brought it in with Joshua when they took possession of the nations”—God Traveled with His People for Centuries
Verse 45: our fathers received this tabernacle in turn and brought it in with Joshua into the Promised Land, where it remained until the days of David.

From the wilderness to Canaan, from Joshua to David, over four hundred years, God’s presence stayed in one tent, at Shiloh, at Kiriath-jearim, moving with the people. In those four hundred years Israel fought wars, worshiped idols, had judges and Saul, and God never said, “Build me a fixed house.” He evidently did not think the tent lacking in anything.
“Received in turn” is a lovely phrase. What one generation handed to the next was not a piece of land but a tent holding God’s word.
• God does not despise the humble tent: what He cares about is presence, not buildings.
• What do we hand on to the next generation: property, scale, reputation, or God’s word and God’s presence?
III. “He asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. But Solomon built him a house”—Man Wants to Pin God Down
Verses 46–47 have a turn. David found favor before God and “asked to find a dwelling place for the God of Jacob.” “But” Solomon built Him a house.

Stephen’s “but” should be read against 2 Samuel 7. David, living in a house of cedar, saw God’s ark still within curtains and wanted to build God a house. That very night God answered through Nathan: “Are you the one to build me a house to dwell in? For I have not lived in a house since the day I brought the children of Israel up out of Egypt, even to this day, but have moved about in a tent and in a tabernacle” (2 Sam. 7:5–6). Then God turned it around: it is not you who will build me a house, but I who will build you a house. David’s heart was good and God accepted his heart, but God said: this is not what I asked for.

The temple was built in the end, God accepted it, and glory filled it. But Stephen’s point is that the temple was never something God initiated; it was man who wanted to “find a dwelling place” for God, to give God a fixed address.

Someone wants to build an aquarium for the ocean and designs it exquisitely—but the ocean cannot fit in an aquarium; only a little seawater does. The intention of building a house for God may be good, but unnoticed one begins to take the house for God Himself and to think He is only there. Later Israel really did think so, crying, “This is the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord” (Jer. 7:4), as if having the temple meant everything was safe.
• Good intentions may also try to pin God down: when you want to do something great for God, first ask whether He wants it.
• Tell temple from God: God is in the temple, but God is not the temple; the church is God’s house, but the church is not God.
IV. “The Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands”—This Is the Word for Idols
Verse 48 is the center of this passage: “However, the Most High doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands.”

“Made with hands” is a single word in the original, used in the Greek Old Testament almost exclusively of idols—the very meaning of “the works of their hands” in verse 41 of the last devotion. When Stephen applied this word to the temple, those in the council must have caught their breath. His meaning was plain: if the temple is treated as where God lives, as security, as proof that you possess God, it changes from God’s house into an idol made by hands, no different from the calf.

This sentence is sharp, yet not new at all. On the day he dedicated the temple Solomon said: “Behold, the heavens and the heaven of heavens can’t contain you; how much less this house which I have built!” (1 Kings 8:27). The builder of the temple knew better than anyone that it could not contain God; those who forgot it were the temple’s later keepers.
• “The Most High”: the title Stephen uses is itself the answer—He is Most High; how could He be contained in something made by hands?
• Examine the temple in your hands: of the church’s buildings, traditions, systems and ministries, which have I taken for God Himself?
V. “Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool”—The Prophet’s Questions

Verses 49–50 quote Isaiah 66: The Lord says, Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool. What kind of house will you build me? Or what is the place of my rest? Didn’t my hand make all these things?

God answers those who want to build Him a house with three questions: What kind of house can you build? Where can the Lord of heaven and earth be set? Aren’t the stones and timber you build with “made by my hand”? What kind of offering is it to make me a dwelling out of what I made?

The very next verse of Isaiah, which Stephen did not quote but which everyone in the council knew: “But to this man will I look, even to him who is humble and contrite in spirit, and who trembles at my word” (Isa. 66:2). The place God truly wants to dwell is not a house of stone but a humble and contrite person. This is just what Stephen will say in the next section: you are “uncircumcised in heart and ears”—the place God wants to dwell, you have not prepared.
• God’s temple is people: “Don’t you know that you are a temple of God, and that God’s Spirit lives in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16).
• What He wants is not a building but a humble and contrite heart: a heart that trembles at God’s word is a better resting place for Him than a magnificent temple.
The Light of the 321 Principles: God Dwells in a Heart Emptied of Self, Not in a House Made by Hands
From tabernacle to temple, Stephen is really speaking of a human tendency: to pin God down so that we can hold Him.

The old self, with its life of self, needs a place that can contain God—a temple, a system, a tradition, a ministry—because a God contained in it can be predicted, managed, and used to secure oneself. But “the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands.” Once a person puts God into something of his own making, that thing becomes an idol. This is pride: leaving one’s place, grasping at power, trying to place God within the range of what man manages.

What God truly wants to dwell in is a humble and contrite heart that trembles at His word—that is, a heart emptied of self. Self-denial is not having nothing; it is making room for oneself to give way, so that the God whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is earth will be pleased to rest here. One who lets Jesus be King is God’s temple; building God’s system is not building a bigger temple but a people like this forming a realm where He can rest.
a: Follow God’s Pattern
Is today’s worship and service what God says He wants, or what I think He should like?
Treasure the Tent
Don’t despise plain gatherings or small fellowships; care only whether God is in the midst.
Ask God First Whether He Wants It
Before doing something great for God, quietly listen to Him.
Take Down the Aquarium
Find the thing you use to “contain God,” and admit that He is greater than that.
Prepare His Resting Place
Tremble once today before God’s word, and give Him a place in your heart to rest.
q: In your faith life, is there something you use to “contain God”—a place, a form, a way of doing things—without which you feel God is absent? God is greater than it: what does this mean for you today?
Isaiah says God looks to the one who is “humble and contrite in spirit, and trembles at my word.” When did you last tremble at God’s word? Does God have a place in your heart to rest right now?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You would rather dwell in a tent of cloth, traveling with Your people, than be fixed in a house of stone; You are the Most High, heaven is Your throne and earth Your footstool, and nothing made by hands can contain You. Thank You for showing us that the place You truly want to dwell is a humble and contrite heart that trembles at Your word.
Lord, we confess that we often want to build You a house so that You will have an address we can hold; we take the church, tradition, systems and ministries for You Yourself, and while guarding them we push You out. Remove the “self” within us that wants to contain You, teach us to tell the temple from You, let You be the Most High and let us return to our place as human beings. Prepare in our hearts a place where You can rest, make us Your temple, and let Your Spirit dwell in us. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: “You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit! As your fathers did, so you do.
Which of the prophets didn’t your fathers persecute? They killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, of whom you have now become betrayers and murderers.
You received the law as it was ordained by angels, and didn’t keep it!”
b: In the last devotion, Stephen quoted Isaiah: heaven is God’s throne, the earth is His footstool, and the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands. This was the summit of the first main theme of his sermon—God is never limited to one place or one temple.

Today’s three verses are the summit of the second main theme and the conclusion of the whole sermon. From verse 2 to verse 50 Stephen kept saying “our fathers”; at verse 51 it suddenly becomes “you”—“As your fathers did, so do you.” He told fifty verses of history, and those in the council may have kept nodding, because it was their history; only at this moment did they realize the mirror was turned toward themselves. Joseph was sold by his brothers, Moses was pushed away by his brothers, the prophets were killed by the fathers—and the Righteous One was betrayed and murdered by you.
I. “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears”—Accusing Those Who Guard Moses with Moses’ Own Words

Every phrase Stephen uses comes from Moses and the prophets. “Stiff-necked” is what God said of Israel at the foot of Sinai after the golden calf (Exod. 33:3, 5)—an ox that will not bow its head to the yoke stiffens its neck; “uncircumcised in heart” is Moses’ word: “Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiff-necked” (Deut. 10:16); “uncircumcised in ears” is Jeremiah’s (Jer. 6:10).

The council accused Stephen of blaspheming Moses, and Stephen answers in Moses’ own words, not a word changed. The meaning is plain: it is not I who am unfaithful to Moses, but you—Moses said long ago that you were stiff-necked, and you still are.

“Uncircumcised in heart and ears” should be read together with verse 8. The covenant of circumcision God gave Abraham was a mark cut in the body; but true circumcision is in the heart and in the ears—whether the heart can be tender, whether the ear can hear. Every person in the council had been circumcised in the body, but not in heart and ears. The outward sign complete, the inward reality absent—this is the deepest trap of religion.
• What stiff-necked looks like: when God’s word touches my wrong, the first reaction is to explain rather than to bow.
• Examine heart and ears: when I hear a sermon, am I listening to what God is saying to me, or judging whether the speaker is right?
II. “You always resist the Holy Spirit! As your fathers did, so you do”—One Sentence to Conclude All of History

In the second half of verse 51 Stephen draws one conclusion about Israel’s history: “You always resist the Holy Spirit.” “Always” is “ever, at every time”; “resist” is “to fall against, to collide head-on.” Not occasional disobedience, but all along, generation after generation, colliding head-on with the Holy Spirit.

This one sentence ties the previous fifty verses together. God delivered through Joseph, and the patriarchs were jealous; God delivered through Moses, and the people pushed him away; God spoke through the prophets, and the fathers persecuted them; God walked with them in a tent, and they carried the calf and Moloch. Every person God sent was sent by the Spirit; every rejection was a resisting of the Holy Spirit. And Stephen himself at this moment was speaking “by the wisdom and the Spirit” (6:10); what the crowd was resisting was also the Holy Spirit.

“As your fathers did, so you do.” This is the most piercing line, because what the council members took pride in all their lives was “we are Abraham’s descendants.” Stephen says: Yes, you are very much like your fathers—in rejecting God.
• What resisting the Spirit looks like: the Spirit touches you through a person, a word, a passage, and you push back head-on, still feeling you are defending the truth.
• Don’t take pride in bloodline or tradition: being like the fathers depends on in what way.
III. “Of whom you have now become betrayers and murderers”—From Joseph to the Righteous One

Verse 52 is a question and a declaration. “Which of the prophets didn’t your fathers persecute?” In Israel’s history almost no prophet was welcomed: Elijah fled for his life, Jeremiah was put in a pit, Uriah was killed, and tradition says Isaiah was sawn in two. The fathers killed “those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One”; and you have “now become betrayers and murderers” of that Righteous One.

“Betrayers” uses the very word of Joseph’s story. The patriarchs sold Joseph to Egypt; you betrayed the Righteous One. “The Righteous One” is a title of the Messiah (Isa. 53:11), which Peter also used in chapter three (Acts 3:14). The two lines of the whole sermon meet here: God is never limited to one place or temple, so He Himself “came down” (7:34) to become the Righteous One; Israel repeatedly rejected those God sent, so they killed the Righteous One. From Joseph, Moses and the prophets the road ran all the way to the cross—not nailed by the fathers, but by “you.”

Some people listen all their lives to others telling the family story, and only at the end discover that the worst character in it is themselves. Stephen’s sermon is such a mirror. But note that he is not settling old scores; he is giving them one last chance—if “betrayers and murderers” were acknowledged, it would become Peter’s Pentecost “What shall we do?” (2:37).
• Bring the focus back to self: when reading about failures in the Bible, don’t ask “how could they be so bad?” but “where am I also like this?”
• Confession is the door to turning back: preaching is never meant to condemn, but to bring people to be cut to the heart and turn.
IV. “You received the law as it was ordained by angels, and did not keep it”—Who Really Despises the Law
Verse 53: Stephen turns the last charge around too. They had accused him of speaking against the law; he says: you received the law as ordained by angels, and did not keep it.

“Ordained by angels” is the Jewish tradition that the law was given to Moses on Sinai through angels (also mentioned in Gal. 3:19 and Heb. 2:2). Stephen uses the phrase to exalt the law—it came from heaven, ordained by angels—and then says: this honored law, you did not keep. Not that you didn’t know it, but you “did not keep” it.

The commonest mistake of those who guard the law is to treat it as a possession rather than a command. They study it, argue it, take pride in it, use it to condemn others, and only fail to obey it. Here both accusations are turned around: you who say I defile the holy place have made the holy place into God; you who say I despise the law have the law and do not keep it.
• Knowing is not keeping: Scripture is my standard means I live by it, not that I have memorized it well.
• The most dangerous step in possessing truth: using it to condemn others while not standing under it oneself.
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Root of Resisting the Spirit Is the Self That Will Not Bow

Stephen speaks very heavily in these three verses, but see his motive: he calls them “brothers and fathers” (7:2), he told fifty verses of family history, and his face still has the look of an angel. This is not hatred but the cry of one who sees his brothers heading for a cliff.

“Stiff-necked” and “resisting the Spirit” describe the outside and the inside of the same thing. The neck is outward, the Spirit inward; the neck is stiff because inside is a self that will not bow. The typical reaction of the old self’s life of self is exactly this: when God touches me through a person, a word, or circumstances, my first move is to push back head-on—with explanations, with arguments, with “I’m doing it for the truth.” Such a person may be in the temple, circumcised, able to recite the law, yet resisting the Holy Spirit all the way.

To make the Holy Spirit my guide presupposes that I am willing to be guided—that the neck will soften, and heart and ears accept circumcision. Humility overcoming pride looks like this: when God’s word touches my wrong, I don’t explain; I bow first. In that bow, Pentecost happens; without it comes what verse 54 describes next, gnashing of teeth. The same sermon, two outcomes, the difference only whether the neck is soft.
a: Soften the Neck
When God’s word touches your wrong today, practice making your first reaction not an explanation but a bow.
Circumcise the Inside
With the outward marks of faith all in place, ask whether heart and ears have been circumcised.
Recognize Whom You Are Resisting
The person or word you keep pushing back at—could the Holy Spirit be touching you through them?
See Yourself in the Failures
Reading about the council and the fathers, don’t ask “how could they be so bad?” but “where am I the same?”
Stand Under the Law
Take the passage you know best and turn it from “I know it” into “I did it today.”
q: “As your fathers did, so do you.” If Stephen said this to you today, at what point would he say you are like those you have always criticized?

Recall the most recent time you “pushed back head-on”—against an exhortation, a passage, a person. Looking back now, could that have been the Holy Spirit touching you? Are you willing to bow once today?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Stephen, unafraid of death, held up that mirror so the council could see “As your fathers did, so do you.” Thank You that today You hold this mirror before us too, that we may not only read others’ history but see where we also are stiff-necked and resist the Holy Spirit.
Lord, we confess that our outward marks are all in place—baptized, in church, reading the Bible—yet heart and ears are often uncircumcised; when Your word touches our wrong, our first move is to explain, argue and push back, and we think we are defending the truth. Remove the “self” within us that will not bow, soften our necks, circumcise our hearts and ears, that we may hear You touching us through people and through Your word. Keep us from being like the fathers, betraying and killing those You send; let us be like the people at Pentecost, cut to the heart, saying, “What shall we do?” In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Now when they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and they gnashed at him with their teeth.
But he, being full of the Holy Spirit, looked up steadfastly into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God,
and said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!”
But they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears, then rushed at him with one accord.
They threw him out of the city and stoned him. The witnesses placed their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.
They stoned Stephen as he called out, saying, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!”
He kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!” When he had said this, he fell asleep.
b: In the last devotion, Stephen’s sermon ended by landing on the members of the Sanhedrin: you stiff-necked people, always resisting the Holy Spirit; your fathers killed the prophets, and you have killed the Righteous One.

That sermon was never finished; what came next was stones. These seven verses are the death of the first martyr in church history. Yet Luke does not write it like an execution but like a coronation—heaven opens, the Lord stands, a man kneels in prayer, and then he “fell asleep.” The two main threads of the whole sermon both reach their end here: God is not confined to one temple, so heaven opened right over the courtroom of the Sanhedrin; Israel kept rejecting those God sent, so they killed this one too.
I. “Cut to the heart, and they gnashed their teeth at him”—One Sermon, Two Endings

In verse 54, “cut to the heart” literally means “sawn through in the heart.” This word was used once in chapter 5—when the Sanhedrin heard Peter say, “The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you killed, hanging him on a tree,” they were also “cut to the heart” (5:33).

Compare chapter 2. On the day of Pentecost, the people heard Peter’s sermon and were “cut to the heart” (2:37), and three thousand were baptized. The same heart-piercing: one pierced and turned back, the other sawn through and furious. The difference was not in the preaching but in whether the hearers were willing to bow their heads. The last devotion said “stiff-necked”; this one shows the result of a stiff neck: gnashing teeth.
God’s word is a two-edged sword: a soft heart is healed by it, a hard heart is enraged by it. A person’s reaction to God’s word exposes not God’s word but the heart.
• Check your reaction when you are pierced: is it a broken heart, or gnashing teeth?
• Fury is the last stop of a stiff neck: one who pushes back all the way ends up with only a fist.
II. “He saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God”—He Has Stood Up

In verses 55 and 56, all around were faces gnashing their teeth, yet Stephen “looked up steadfastly into heaven.” He saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God, and said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!”

Three things to notice. First, “the glory of God”—Stephen’s very first sentence in the sermon was that the “God of glory” appeared to Abraham in Mesopotamia (7:2); now the God of glory appears to him in the courtroom in Jerusalem. Not in the temple, but in the Sanhedrin. The first thread is fulfilled here completely: wherever heaven opens, that is holy ground.

Second, “standing at the right hand of God.” Throughout Scripture Jesus is said to be “seated” at God’s right hand—sitting means the work is finished. Only here is He “standing.” Some say He stood up as Stephen’s advocate: the earthly court pronounced him guilty, and the heavenly court stood to testify for him; others say He stood to welcome him—like a father who hears his son push open the door and rises from his chair. When his child has run the hardest stretch outside, a father does not stay seated.

Third, “the Son of Man.” Outside the four Gospels, only Stephen uses this title. A few months earlier, Jesus said in this very Sanhedrin, “You will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power” (Mark 14:62), and the high priest tore his clothes and condemned Him to death. Now Stephen says: I see Him.
• Look up steadfastly into heaven: when all around are hostile faces, lift your eyes—heaven is open.
• He stands for you: when you are condemned and misunderstood on earth, there is a Lord standing in heaven.
III. “They stopped their ears and rushed at him with one accord”—Those with Uncircumcised Ears Cover Their Ears
Verse 57: the people cried out with a loud voice, stopped their ears, and rushed at him with one accord.

“Stopped their ears”—in the last devotion Stephen had just said their “hearts and ears are uncircumcised,” and here they cover their ears with their hands. Those who resist the Holy Spirit end up unwilling even to listen. They “cried out with a loud voice,” drowning God’s word with their own voices; “with one accord”—these Pharisees and Sadducees, usually at odds with each other, were united in killing the one God had sent.

Then verse 58: “They threw him out of the city and stoned him.” The law said a blasphemer must be stoned outside the camp (Lev. 24:14), and they evidently thought they were carrying out the law. But the law also required a death sentence to follow a trial, and the Romans did not allow the Jews to put anyone to death privately—this very act of “enforcing the law” was itself lawless. The man just accused of “not keeping the law” indeed was the one who kept it, while they did not.
• What covering your ears looks like: not reading that passage, not taking that call—because you know you will be touched.
• Unity in wrong is not unity: people of self joining together only do a greater wrong together.
IV. “The witnesses laid down their clothes at the feet of a young man named Saul”—A Seed Falls
In the second half of verse 58, Luke quietly adds one line: the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.

The witnesses had to throw the first stones (Deut. 17:7), so they took off their outer garments and laid them at a young man’s feet to guard. This young man was from Tarsus in Cilicia, and was probably one of those in the Cilician synagogue of 6:9 who could not out-argue Stephen. He stood there, watching, listening, consenting.

Luke’s way of writing is almost a whisper, but everyone who has read Acts knows the weight of this line. Stephen’s sermon and his dying prayer—Saul missed not a word. A few years later, on the road to Damascus, the Lord who stood asked him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” Where Stephen fell, a grain of wheat fell into the ground.
• God did not waste that day: Stephen could not see what fruit his death would bear, but God saw.
• Someone is watching your witness: not necessarily the friendliest person, but he is listening, and God will use it.
V. “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” “Don’t hold this sin against them”—Dying Like the Lord

In verses 59 and 60, as the stones fell, Stephen made two prayers. The first: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!” The second, “he cried with a loud voice”, kneeling down: “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!” Then Luke writes: “When he had said this, he fell asleep.”

Anyone who has read Luke recognizes these two sentences at once: Jesus on the cross said, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit!” (Luke 23:46), and “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Stephen almost repeated the Lord’s words verbatim, only changing “Father” to “Lord Jesus”—the One to whom he committed his spirit was the One he had just seen standing.

Jesus is my example, and the most complete demonstration is right here. This is not imitation but the same life being lived out in another person—not I who live, but Christ lives in me. A man who, while being stoned to death, can still ask forgiveness for those stoning him has no “self” left inside that needs protecting; he could kneel because he knew who was standing.
“Fell asleep”—Luke does not say “died.” For a believer, death is sleep; and one who sleeps will wake.
• Commit your spirit to Him: don’t wait until the deathbed—say today, “Lord Jesus, receive me.”
• Ask forgiveness for those who hurt you: this is not self-cultivation but evidence that the Lord lives in you.
The Light of the 321 Principles: For the One Emptied of Self, Heaven Opens

From the time he was chosen to serve tables (6:5) to kneeling under the stones, Luke gives Stephen only one description: “full of the Holy Spirit.” He was when serving tables, when debating, and when dying.

A person full of the Holy Spirit is a person of self-denial—inside him there is no “self” that wants to protect itself, prove itself, or take revenge. So when the stones struck, his reaction was not hatred but kneeling in prayer; while all around gnashed their teeth, his eyes were on heaven. Self-denial is not nothingness but entering the infinite: what Stephen lost was one life; what he gained was an open heaven, a standing Lord, and a young man named Saul—who later carried the gospel to Rome.

Letting Jesus be King, taken to its extreme, means placing even death in His hands; letting Jesus receive all the glory, taken to its extreme, means that when a person dies, no one remembers how well he could preach—everyone sees heaven opened. And building God’s system is just this: grain by grain falling into the ground—not by organization, but by people like Stephen who, when pushed outside the city, still ask forgiveness for those pushing him.
a: Check Your Reaction When Pierced
When God’s word pierces you, choose a broken heart, not gnashing teeth.
Practice Looking Up
When you meet a hostile face today, lift your eyes and remember there is a Lord who stands.
Don’t Cover Your Ears
That passage you have not dared to read, that exhortation you did not want to hear—open it and listen today.
Believe the Seed Will Sprout
Your witness—the most unlikely person is listening.
Speak Like the Lord
Toward the one who hurt you, say once in prayer today, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against him.”
q: Stephen’s two dying prayers were verbatim the Lord Jesus’ words on the cross. Is there someone in your life of whom you still cannot say today, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against him”? What is holding you back?

Saul stood by, watching, listening, consenting. Think: is there a “Saul” near you—the most unlikely person, even one who opposes you? Are you willing to believe that your witness today is falling into his heart?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that in a Sanhedrin of gnashing teeth You opened heaven, and in a courtroom of condemnation Your Son stood up. Thank You for letting us see that wherever You appear is holy ground, and that those You sent were rejected, pushed away, and killed all along the way, yet You were with them all the way.
Lord Jesus, we confess that there is still too much inside us that wants to protect itself—wanting to defend when misunderstood, to remember when hurt, to push back when pierced. Fill us as You filled Stephen, remove the “self” that will not kneel, so that when stones fall we still look up to heaven and still ask forgiveness for others. Lord, today we commit our spirits into Your hands, not waiting for the deathbed; and take our whole life as a grain of wheat, to fall where You want it, to bear fruit we cannot see but You can. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Saul was consenting to his death. A great persecution arose against the assembly which was in Jerusalem in that day. They were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except for the apostles.
Devout men buried Stephen and lamented greatly over him.
But Saul ravaged the assembly, entering into every house and dragged both men and women off to prison.
Therefore those who were scattered abroad went around preaching the word.
Philip went down to the city of Samaria, and proclaimed to them the Christ.
The multitudes listened with one accord to the things that were spoken by Philip when they heard and saw the signs which he did.
For unclean spirits came out of many of those who had them. They came out, crying with a loud voice. Many who had been paralyzed and lame were healed.
There was great joy in that city.
b: In the last devotion, Stephen knelt under the stones, committed his spirit to the Lord, asked forgiveness for those who struck him, and then “fell asleep.” At the edge of that scene Luke recorded a name: the witnesses laid their clothes at the feet of a young man named Saul.

At the beginning of chapter 8 the camera stays on this man. From that day, a great persecution arose against the church and the disciples were scattered. It looked as if Satan had won a round, but Luke wants us to see something else—what the stones scattered was in fact a handful of seed.
I. “Saul was consenting to his death”—A Man Standing on the Other Side Is Recorded by Name

The first half of verse 1: “Saul was consenting to his death.” “Consenting” in the original means “approving together, agreeing in heart.” Saul did not throw stones, only guarded the clothes; but his heart stood on the same side as the throwing hands. He later admitted it himself: “When the blood of Stephen your witness was shed, I also was standing by and consenting” (Acts 22:20). Luke does not cover for him, nor does he write him off. This name first appears in the church’s story standing on the other side; one chapter later, he will fall to the ground on the road to Damascus.

The second half of verse 1: “A great persecution arose against the assembly which was in Jerusalem. They were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except for the apostles.” Interestingly, “except for the apostles”: those who stayed in Jerusalem were the leaders, and those scattered everywhere were the ordinary disciples. The ones who next carried the gospel out of Jerusalem were not the Twelve but these nameless brothers and sisters.
• The ending is not written at the first appearance: in God’s story, even those on the other side have names.
• Those who went out were ordinary believers: God’s system is not held up by a few leaders but by every person.
II. “Devout men buried Stephen… but Saul ravaged the assembly”—Two Pairs of Hands
Verses 2 and 3 place two pictures side by side.

The first: “Devout men buried Stephen and lamented greatly over him.” By the custom of the time, a person condemned and executed by the Sanhedrin was not to be publicly mourned. Yet these people wept aloud—a public stand: we do not accept that verdict. Burying a man who had been stoned to death was risky, and they took the risk.

The second: “But Saul ravaged the assembly, entering into every house, and dragging both men and women, he committed them to prison.” The word “ravaged” in the original describes a wild beast tearing at its prey. Saul broke in house after house, sparing not even women. The first assault the church suffered was not from a Gentile government but from the most zealous one among their own, tearing with religious zeal.

Same city, same day: one pair of hands burying and weeping, another seizing and dragging. Luke sets them side by side so we see clearly: persecution most often comes from “zeal.” Saul was not ungodly; he was too devout—devout by his own standard. The hotter the zeal of self, the more fearful it is; it takes its own righteousness for God’s righteousness. What it looks like today: when I am zealous for the Lord, if I grow less and less able to tolerate people, that zeal is probably already “mine,” not His.
• Weeping is allowed: the church did not pretend to be strong; this mourning was also faith.
• Zeal must be tested for its source: zeal standing on one’s own righteousness tears people; zeal standing on the Lord’s righteousness lifts them up.
III. “Those who were scattered went around preaching”—What the Stones Scattered Was Seed
Verse 4: “Therefore those who were scattered abroad went around preaching the word.”

The word “scattered,” Luke uses only three times in his writings (8:1, 8:4, 11:19), all about this persecution. Its root means “sowing seed”—the motion of a farmer scattering seed from his hand. The persecutors thought they were smashing the church; in God’s eyes, it was a hand sowing.

Think of a dandelion. If it stays safely rooted where it is, it is one plant for life; only when the wind blows does it fill the whole hillside. The disciples were gathered nicely in Jerusalem—but what the Lord said in chapter 1 was “in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” By chapter 8 they had not yet left Jerusalem. So God allowed a wind to blow.

“Went around preaching the word”—in the original, “announcing the good news.” They did not flee in complaint but spoke wherever they went. This is what a focus on Jesus rather than circumstances looks like: homes ransacked, yet the good news still in their mouths.
• Scattering is sowing: the persecutor’s hand became a farmer’s hand in God’s hand.
• Circumstances change the address, not the direction: what is in your mouth is not decided by circumstances.
IV. “Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed the Christ”—The Gospel Crosses the Oldest Wall
Verse 5: “Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed the Christ to them.”

This Philip is not the apostle Philip of the Twelve but one of the seven chosen in chapter 6 to oversee the distribution of food, later called “Philip the evangelist” (Acts 21:8). When the tables were scattered, he became a preacher. God’s work does not follow personnel orders: wherever the Holy Spirit places an obedient person, that is his harvest field.

He went to Samaria, the oldest wall in Jewish hearts. The Samaritans were descendants of the northern kingdom’s survivors who intermarried with foreigners; they had their own temple and their own Pentateuch, and the Jews considered them unclean—“Jews have no dealings with Samaritans” (John 4:9). A man from Jerusalem going to Samaria to preach Christ was almost unthinkable to Jews. Yet the Lord had named Samaria back in chapter 1, and He Himself had said to a Samaritan woman at Jacob’s well, “I am he.” The first to truly cross this wall was not an apostle but a deacon driven out by persecution.
“Proclaimed the Christ”—he did not preach the political hope Samaritans liked to hear, nor his own experience, but Christ.
• Ministries change, obedience does not: wherever the Lord puts you is the harvest field.
• Cross that wall: the gospel’s route often passes through the place in my heart I least want to go.
V. “There was great joy in that city”—The Transformation of a City

Verses 6 to 8: the crowds “paid attention with one accord to the things that were spoken by Philip.” This is a phrase Luke often uses for the Jerusalem church (1:14, 2:46, 4:24); now it is used of Samaritans: that despised people also listened with one heart. Unclean spirits came out “crying with a loud voice”—the powers of darkness do not leave quietly; they cry out, but they must go. The paralyzed and lame were healed. Then Luke closes: “There was great joy in that city.”

Put verse 1 and verse 8 together: great persecution in Jerusalem, great joy in Samaria. One persecution, two cities; the tears of one city became the joy of the other. Satan wanted to seal off the gospel with persecution, but God used the same persecution to carry the gospel across a wall no one had crossed for centuries. People see loss; God sees sowing. People count how many were scattered; God counts which fields they fell into.
• Darkness cries out, but it must go: once Christ is proclaimed, it has to leave.
• Tears and joy share one source: the mourning in that city became joy in this one in God’s hand.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Focus on Jesus, Not on Circumstances
The first eight verses of chapter 8 are a road from tears to joy.

The disciples did not choose this road. They did not hold a meeting and resolve to “do missions in Samaria”; they were struck out by persecution. But one thing was not struck out of them: the good news in their mouths. Their focus was not on circumstances—homes ransacked, friends dead, Saul chasing behind—but on Jesus. For a person whose focus is on Jesus, circumstances can change his address but cannot change his direction.

This also shows us that building God’s system is not building a fixed structure. However wonderful the gathering in Jerusalem, if it stayed there forever it would become a place no one wanted to leave, not a people going to the ends of the earth. God’s system is a people who let Jesus be King—wherever they go, that realm expands. Change from the human view to God’s view: that thing happening to you today that “scatters” you may well be the Lord’s hand sowing.
a: Test the Source of Your Zeal
Zeal standing on your own righteousness tears people; zeal standing on the Lord’s righteousness lifts them up.
Allow Yourself to Weep
Devout men wept aloud for Stephen; mourning is not unbelief but honesty.
See Scattering as Sowing
What is scattering you today may be God sowing you into a new field.
Speak Wherever You Go
Circumstances changed the address; don’t let them change the good news in your mouth.
Cross That Wall
Ask yourself: where is the “Samaria” in my heart? The Lord wants me to go there.
q: Recall one time in your life when you were “scattered”—a move, a loss, a broken relationship, a plan torn down. Looking back, did God “sow” you into a field you would not otherwise have gone to?
Saul’s persecution came out of zeal. When you are zealous for the Lord, have you become unable to tolerate certain people? Whose righteousness is that zeal standing on right now?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that what the stones scattered was in fact a handful of seed in Your hand. Thank You for letting us see that the tears of Jerusalem became the joy of Samaria, and the road Satan wanted to seal was opened by You. Your hand has never left this situation; even one standing on the other side, You recorded his name.
Lord Jesus, we confess that we often put our focus on circumstances: when things change, our hearts are troubled; when our home is shaken, the good news in our mouths disappears. Turn our eyes back to You, so that in days of scattering we still speak wherever we go. And search our zeal: if, like Saul, we are zealous for You standing on our own righteousness, stop us and bring us back to our place. Show us where the oldest wall in our hearts is, and give us Philip’s obedience to go there and proclaim Christ. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: But there was a certain man, Simon by name, who used to practice sorcery in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, making himself out to be some great one,
to whom they all listened, from the least to the greatest, saying, “This man is that great power of God.”
They listened to him, because for a long time he had amazed them with his sorceries.
But when they believed Philip preaching good news concerning God’s Kingdom and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women.
Simon himself also believed. Being baptized, he continued with Philip. Seeing signs and great miracles occurring, he was amazed.
b: In the last devotion, Philip went down to Samaria and proclaimed Christ; unclean spirits came out, the sick were healed, and “there was great joy in that city.”

Luke then pulls the camera back: before Philip arrived, this city already had a “great man.” His name was Simon. The whole city had followed him for a long time; young and old listened to him and called him “the great power of God.” Then the gospel came, and the city turned; even Simon himself was baptized. But Luke leaves a thread hanging on him—he believed, was baptized, and then was “amazed.” These five verses help us tell two things apart: being drawn to great power and letting the Great One be King are not the same thing.
I. “Making himself out to be some great one”—A Man Who Talked Himself Up
Verse 9: “There was a certain man, Simon by name, who used to practice sorcery in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, making himself out to be some great one.”

“Practice sorcery” translates the word “magus”—the same word as the “wise men” from the east in Matthew. Such men did well in that world: a little astronomy, a little medicine, a few spells, plus a talent for performance, and they could get a whole city following. “Making himself out to be some great one” literally means “saying of himself that he was somebody great.” Luke writes it precisely: he was not truly great; he “said” he was great.

This is the archetype of pride. Pride is not a bad temper or a loud voice; pride is leaving one’s place—one who is created and limited, by various means presenting himself as unlimited, powerful, and worthy of being looked up to. Simon used sorcery; we may use résumés, eloquence, spiritual vocabulary; the methods differ, the motion is the same: talking oneself up. What it looks like today: when I introduce myself before people, have I quietly added a few points?
• Not truly great, but “saying” he was great: the essence of pride is self-inflation, not actual weight.
• Talking yourself up is leaving your place: the created trying to be the Creator is the root of every problem.
II. “This man is that great power of God”—A City That Took a Man for God

Verses 10 and 11: “They all listened to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, ‘This man is that great power of God.’ They listened to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his sorceries.”

For a man to talk himself up is not enough; a city must be willing to treat him as great. “From the least to the greatest”—regardless of age or class, the whole city heeded him. The title they gave him was “that great power of God”—that is, “the power of God itself.” For a man to be taken as the power of God was not strange to Samaritans—their faith had long mixed in foreign elements, and they were used to looking for God in people.

Luke points out why they followed: “because for a long time he had amazed them.” The word “amazed” appears three times in these five verses (verses 9, 11, 13) and is the key word of the passage. The rope tying the whole city to Simon was not truth but amazement. Amazement makes people follow but does not make them change. A city can be drawn by one man’s performance for a long time—“for a long time” he used sorceries, for years, and not one life was healed, not one unclean spirit cast out.

Think of fireworks and sunrise. When fireworks go off the whole sky cheers, but three seconds later nothing is left; the sunrise is far quieter—no one applauds—but once it rises, the whole city has daylight. Simon was the fireworks, and the people of the city were used to looking up and waiting for the next burst; what Philip brought was the sunrise.
• Amazement is not truth: what makes people cheer may not heal them.
• Looking for God in a person is dangerous: anyone who puts “the great power of God” on his own head is not God.
III. “They believed Philip preaching good news concerning the Kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ”—A City Turned
Verse 12: “But when they believed Philip preaching good news concerning the Kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women.”

When Luke writes the transformation of this city, he does not use “they were more amazed” but “they believed.” The content of belief is stated clearly: “the Kingdom of God” and “the name of Jesus Christ.” The Kingdom of God—the realm where God reigns as King; the name of Jesus Christ—the King Himself. What Philip preached in this city was just what the Lord spoke of for forty days after His resurrection (Acts 1:3). He did not compete with Simon over whose performance was more impressive; he preached a King.

“Both men and women were baptized.” Baptism is a public act: I come out from my former belonging and enter into this name. This city originally belonged under Simon; now, one by one, they came out from there and entered under the name of Jesus Christ. From being bound by amazement to letting Jesus be King—this is a city’s real transformation, not swapping for a more impressive idol but changing the Lord.

Change the concept and you change life. The Samaritans’ old concept was: the power is in that great man, follow him and you’re fine; now the concept changed: the King is Jesus, and the power is His. Life followed by changing belonging, and living was baptized along with it.
• From amazement to belief: not being drawn more strongly, but placing oneself under one name.
• What changed is not the idol but the Lord: real transformation is a change in who is King.
IV. “Simon himself also believed… and was amazed”—What Did He Believe?
Verse 13: “Simon himself also believed. Being baptized, he continued with Philip. Seeing signs and great miracles occurring, he was amazed.”

Luke gives Simon three actions: believed, was baptized, continued with Philip. From the outside, this is a complete conversion. But at the end of the sentence Luke puts that key word again: “he was amazed.” Before, he amazed the people; now he himself is amazed. He went from the performer to the audience—yet he still stood on the line of “amazement,” not crossing over to the line of “submission.” What he saw were “signs and great miracles,” and power was still what attracted him; in the next passage we will see him try to buy that power with money.

This verse is a mirror for us. A person can believe, be baptized, and follow a preacher every day, while what his heart truly looks up to is still power, gifts, spiritual performance, and not the King. A life of self, even entering the church, will pursue the gospel as a higher kind of power—it still wants to be “great,” only from a different source. A life of self-denial is different: it no longer asks, “How can I get this power?” but only, “How do I obey this King?” What it looks like today: do I read the Bible, pray, and gather because I want to get something, or because I want to give myself to Someone?
• Amazement follows you into church: believing and being baptized, one’s heart may still look up to power, not the King.
• From audience to servant: not standing in the stands cheering, but kneeling before the Lord.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Pride Talks Itself Up; Humility Lets God Be God
In these five verses two kinds of “greatness” are set side by side.

Simon’s greatness was “spoken.” He made himself out to be the great power of God, and a city followed by treating him as God. This is pride—leaving the creature’s place, grasping a position that isn’t one’s own, wanting to replace God. Pride always needs an audience, needs amazement, needs people looking up.

Philip’s greatness was not in himself. What he preached was the Kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ; people believed in that name, not in Philip. This is humility—laying down power, returning to one’s place, letting God be God and man be man. Philip did the same “amazing” things Simon did, but he pointed people to Another; Simon pointed them to himself.

And Simon’s “amazement” after baptism warns us: pursuing power in the church can also be pride in a different coat. Self-denial is not not wanting power but no longer making power the goal—the focus is not on power but on Jesus; not on how much I can get but on whether He can be King in me. Letting Jesus receive all the glory means, every time people are amazed, pointing their eyes to Him.
a: Examine Your “Saying”
Before people, have I made myself sound a bit bigger than I am?
Tell Amazement from Truth
What makes me cheer isn’t necessarily what heals me.
Enter That Name
Real transformation is not swapping for a more impressive idol but changing the Lord.
From Audience to Servant
Do I follow the Lord to get power, or to obey Him?
Point Their Eyes to Him
Every time you are praised, turn that praise back to the Lord.
q: Think honestly: in your life of faith, what attracts you most? If miracles, gifts, and feelings were all taken away, leaving only obedience to the King, would you still be as eager as you are now?
Has there been an occasion when others were “amazed” and praised you, and you kept the glory for yourself? Next time, how could you turn it back to the Lord?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that a city that had followed a sorcerer for years turned to You through the gospel of the Kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ. Thank You that Your power needs no performance; Your sunrise rises quietly, and the whole city has daylight.
Lord Jesus, we confess that there is a Simon in us too, who likes to talk himself up, likes to be looked up to, and chases power more than we seek You. Forgive us, and bring us from the line of “amazement” to the line of “submission,” so that we no longer stand in the stands watching but kneel before You. Remove the heart in us that pursues the gospel as a higher power, and let us want You alone as King. And use us, like Philip, so that every time people see something in us, we point their eyes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Now when the apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them,
who, when they had come down, prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit;
for as yet he had fallen on none of them. They had only been baptized in the name of Christ Jesus.
Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.
Now when Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money,
saying, “Give me also this power, that whomever I lay my hands on may receive the Holy Spirit.”
But Peter said to him, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money!
You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart isn’t right before God.
Repent therefore of this, your wickedness, and ask God if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you.
For I see that you are in the poison of bitterness and in the bondage of iniquity.”
Simon answered, “Pray for me to the Lord, that none of the things which you have spoken happen to me.”
They therefore, when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem, and preached the Good News to many villages of the Samaritans.
b: In the last devotion, the city of Samaria turned, and even Simon, “the great power of God,” was baptized—but he still stayed on the line of “amazement,” looking up to power, not to the King.

In this passage, the thread is pulled. The apostles come from Jerusalem, the Holy Spirit falls, Simon sees it, and he reaches for his money. Peter’s answer is among the sternest words in the whole book of Acts. This passage shows us how God’s gift is given, and what a heart that is “not right” looks like.
I. “They sent Peter and John to them”—The One Who Wanted to Call Down Fire Now Lays On Hands
Verse 14: “Now when the apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them.”

Notice who was sent: John. Years earlier, when a Samaritan village would not receive the Lord, this same John and his brother asked the Lord, “Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from the sky, and destroy them?” (Luke 9:54). The Lord rebuked them. Now the same John walks into Samaria, not to call down fire but to lay on hands and pray, that these people might receive the Holy Spirit.

This is what a person changed by the Lord looks like. The zeal did not lessen, but the direction turned completely around: from burning people to blessing them. What self-denial looks like in John is—the very people he once despised, he now lays his hands on their heads.
• The Lord changes direction, not heat: zeal may stay; the aim must change.
• My “Samaritan village”: the people I once wanted to call fire down on, the Lord may be sending me to lay hands on.
II. “Prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit”—A Special Delay

Verses 15 to 17: “who, when they had come down, prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit; for as yet he had fallen on none of them. They had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.”

These verses often puzzle people: they had already believed and been baptized, so why had the Spirit not yet fallen? Throughout Acts, the way the Holy Spirit comes on people is not uniform—at Pentecost He fell while they were praying, at Cornelius’ house He fell while Peter was still preaching, but here He waited for the apostles to lay on hands. God is not bound by a formula.

Why wait this time? The answer likely lies in the word “Samaria.” Jews and Samaritans had been separated for centuries, each with their own temple. If the Spirit had simply fallen on the Samaritans on their own after they believed, two churches might have appeared, continuing to have no dealings with each other. God let the Spirit wait, until the apostles from Jerusalem came in person and laid their hands on them—this pair of hands was a bridge. From then on the believers of both places were one body, not two.

This shows how much God values unity: He would rather delay the Holy Spirit’s coming for a few days than let His household divide into two. God’s system is a realm formed by people who let Jesus be King, and in this realm there can be no walls.
• God is not bound by formulas: His works have order but are not mechanical.
• The delay was for unity: God would rather wait than have His house divided in two.
III. “Give me also this power”—What Was He Trying to Buy?

Verses 18 and 19: “Now when Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, saying, ‘Give me also this power, that whoever I lay my hands on may receive the Holy Spirit.’”

All his life Simon had made deals: learn a trick, trade it for people’s amazement. Seeing the Holy Spirit given when the apostles laid on hands, he instinctively reached for money. Notice what he wanted—not “Please lay hands on me so that I may receive the Holy Spirit,” but “Give me this power, that whoever I lay my hands on may receive the Holy Spirit.” What he wanted was not to be filled with the Spirit but to control the Spirit; not to be a servant but to be the one with authority to distribute. He wanted to get back on the stage.

In history, buying church office with money is called “simony,” named from here. But this sin does not require pulling out silver. Anyone who tries to use what is his own—giving, seniority, good deeds, years of service—to exchange for God’s gifts and position has the same heart. The deepest instinct of a life of self is to “take hold.”

Think of a concert. You can buy a ticket, even a front-row seat, but you cannot buy the voice on the stage. The voice is given, not sold. So is the Holy Spirit—He is given freely; people can only receive, not purchase, much less resell.
• He wanted control, not to be filled: one who wants to be the distributor, not the recipient.
• You can buy a ticket but not the voice: gifts are given, and every heart that wants to “trade” has come to the wrong door.
IV. “Your heart isn’t right before God”—Peter’s Diagnosis

Verses 20 to 23, Peter said: “Your silver perish with you, because you thought that you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart isn’t right before God. Repent therefore of this, your wickedness, and ask the Lord if perhaps the thought of your heart will be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bondage of iniquity.”

Peter’s words are heavy, but each is a diagnosis, not a curse. “Gift” in the original means “free present”—once a present is priced, it is no longer a present. “Not right” in the original is “not straight”: a heart bent toward itself cannot straighten to face God. “Gall of bitterness” echoes Deuteronomy—describing a root of poison in the heart that grows bitter herbs and wormwood (Deut. 29:18); “bondage of iniquity” echoes the “bands of wickedness” in Isaiah (Isa. 58:6). The Simon Peter saw was not a new believer who made a small mistake but a man with a poison root inside, bound by cords.

But notice that Peter did not close the door: “Repent… ask the Lord if perhaps the thought of your heart will be forgiven you.” The way is still there, if he will turn. “The thought of your heart”—the problem was not the silver but the thing he was thinking in his heart.
• A gift cannot be priced: once priced, the gift becomes a transaction, and the recipient becomes a buyer.
• A bent heart cannot straighten: a heart bent toward itself cannot stand straight before God.
V. “Pray for me to the Lord”—A Half-Step of Repentance, and the Villages on the Way Back
Verse 24: “Simon answered, ‘Pray for me to the Lord, that none of the things which you have spoken happen to me.’”

This sounds like repentance, but looking closely one thing is missing. Peter told him to “repent” and to “ask the Lord” himself; his answer was “you pray for me.” What he feared was the consequence, not grief over his wrong heart. He asked others to pray for him and did not himself turn to the Lord. Luke does not write his end; the man simply stops at a half-step, leaving every reader to think: is my repentance fear of consequences, or hatred of sin itself?

Verse 25: Luke turns the camera back to the apostles: “They, when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem, and preached the Good News to many villages of the Samaritans.” The John who once wanted to call fire down on a Samaritan village now preached good news village by village on the way back. Luke does not stop at one man’s failure but at the gospel moving on.
• Repentance means kneeling yourself: asking others to pray cannot replace turning to the Lord yourself.
• Fearing consequences is not hating sin: true repentance grieves that one’s heart was bent, not just fears punishment.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Gifts Can Only Be Received, Not Grasped
The center of this passage is the motion of a man reaching for money.

Simon’s problem was not lack of zeal but wanting to “grasp” the Holy Spirit. A life of self facing God’s gift has a first reaction: “How do I get it, how do I keep it in my hand?”; a life of self-denial has only one reaction: receive, then let Him be King. The former treats the Spirit as a tool; the latter treats himself as a vessel.

Rely on the Spirit with the heart, not on yourself with the head—Simon calculated a deal with his head, and Peter saw that his “heart was not right.” A person who uses his heart makes no deals; he knows everything is received freely, so he doesn’t want to buy or to sell, only to give thanks.

And the apostles’ laying on of hands tells us something else: God was willing to adjust even the timing of the Spirit’s coming, so that His household would not divide into two. Those who let Jesus be King are bound to be united; in a united church, there is no hand stretched out for itself.
a: Change Direction
The one I wanted to “call fire down” on—the Lord may be sending me to lay hands on and pray for him.
Value Unity
God would rather delay grace for a few days than let His house divide in two; so should I.
Stop Trading
Am I trying to use giving, seniority, or service to “exchange” for God’s gifts or position?
Straighten the Heart
A heart bent toward self cannot stand straight; today turn it back to face God.
Kneel Yourself
Don’t only ask others to pray; true repentance is turning to the Lord yourself.
q: Is there a “what-for-what” mentality hidden in your service or prayer? (For example: I have done so much, so God should give me…) Say it out loud and hand it to the Lord.

Simon said, “Pray for me to the Lord,” yet did not turn to God himself. Recall your most recent confession of sin: was it fear of consequences, or hatred of sin? Did you ask others to pray, or kneel yourself?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Your gift is given freely, and cannot be bought or sold. Thank You that You would rather let the Holy Spirit’s coming wait a few days than fail to make the Samaritans and the Jerusalem believers one body; thank You for changing a John who wanted to call down fire into a John who laid hands on Samaritans.
Lord Jesus, we confess that there is Simon’s calculation in us too—wanting to trade our giving for Your grace, wanting to grasp power more than be filled by You. Search our hearts, and where they bend toward ourselves, straighten them, that we may stand upright before You. Let our repentance be not only fear of consequences but real grief over the thoughts of our hearts, kneeling before You ourselves. And cause us to value the unity of Your house more than our own gifts and positions. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: But an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, “Arise, and go toward the south to the way that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza. This is a desert.”
He arose and went; and behold, there was a man of Ethiopia, a eunuch of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was over all her treasure, who had come to Jerusalem to worship.
He was returning and sitting in his chariot, and was reading the prophet Isaiah.
The Spirit said to Philip, “Go near, and join yourself to this chariot.”
Philip ran to him, and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and said, “Do you understand what you are reading?”
He said, “How can I, unless someone explains it to me?” He begged Philip to come up and sit with him.
Now the passage of the Scripture which he was reading was this, “He was led as a sheep to the slaughter. As a lamb before his shearer is silent, so he doesn’t open his mouth.
In his humiliation, his judgment was taken away. Who will declare His generation? For his life is taken from the earth.”
The eunuch answered Philip, “Who is the prophet talking about? About himself, or about someone else?”
Philip opened his mouth, and beginning from this Scripture, preached to him about Jesus.
As they went on the way, they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “Behold, here is water. What is keeping me from being baptized?”
He commanded the chariot to stand still, and they both went down into the water, both Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him.
When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away, and the eunuch didn’t see him any more, for he went on his way rejoicing.
But Philip was found at Azotus. Passing through, he preached the Good News to all the cities, until he came to Caesarea.
b: In the last devotion, the apostles went back to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel in Samaritan villages along the way; Simon stopped at a half-step of repentance, while Philip stayed in that city of great joy.

Then an angel of the Lord said to Philip something almost unreasonable: leave this city and go to a road in the wilderness—for one person. This is the most beautiful personal evangelism in Acts, and the clearest picture of “the Holy Spirit is my guide, the Bible is my standard.”
I. “Arise and go toward the south… This is a desert”—From a City to an Empty Road

The first half of verses 26 and 27: “But an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, ‘Arise and go toward the south to the way that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.’ This is a desert. He arose and went.”

Luke notes especially: “This is a desert.” The southern road from Jerusalem to Gaza passes through the wilderness of the Judean hills, with no towns and no crowds. Philip had just experienced a whole city turning to the Lord, and now was sent to an empty road; the angel did not tell him why, nor whom he would meet. His response was just three words: “He arose and went.”

This is what the obedience of self-denial looks like in life: no need to know the reason first, no need to calculate whether it is worth it. From a city full of people to a road with none—by the human view a demotion, by God’s view a sending. A person of self measures ministry by scale—how many people, how big the scene; a person of self-denial measures ministry by one thing—where the Lord tells me to go.
