• Obedience doesn’t need to see results first: “He arose and went”; the Lord gives the reason on the road.
• One person is worth a road: God’s sending is not counted by scale; He values one person.
II. “An Ethiopian, a eunuch of great authority”—A Man Who Went Up to Jerusalem but Could Not Enter the Temple

Verses 27 and 28: “Behold, there was a man of Ethiopia, a eunuch of great authority under Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was over all her treasure, who had come to Jerusalem to worship. He was returning and sitting in his chariot, and was reading the prophet Isaiah.”

Ethiopia is the Old Testament Cush, south of Egypt, to people then something like “the ends of the earth.” “Candace” is not a personal name but the title of that country’s queen. This man was the queen’s finance minister: wealth, power, a chariot, a scroll—but he was a eunuch. By the law of Moses, “He who is wounded in the stones, or has his private part cut off, shall not enter into the assembly of Yahweh” (Deut. 23:1). He made the long journey to Jerusalem to worship, yet could not enter the inner courts of the temple. He feared God, but God’s house was shut to him.

So what was he reading on the way home? Isaiah. And in Isaiah there is a word spoken precisely to him: “Don’t let the eunuch say, ‘Behold, I am a dry tree’… I will give them in my house and within my walls a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters” (Isa. 56:3–5). This man walked the wilderness road with a rejected heart, yet in his hands was a scroll that promised him. God was already at work in him; only someone to explain it was missing.
• God sees the one shut outside the door: the temple door was shut, but heaven’s door was not.
• God sends someone to those who seek: the scroll he was reading had already prepared the answer for him.
III. “Do you understand what you are reading?”—The Spirit Guides, Scripture Is the Standard

Verses 29 to 35 are the heart of this narrative. “The Spirit said to Philip, ‘Go near, and join yourself to this chariot.’ Philip ran to him… and said, ‘Do you understand what you are reading?’ He said, ‘How can I, unless someone explains it to me?’”

Look at the order here. The angel first gave a general direction: go south. On the road, the Spirit gave the next sentence: go near the chariot. Philip “ran”—a deacon who started out managing food, running after the carriage of a high official. The Spirit’s guidance is like navigation: it doesn’t describe the whole route at once, only the next turn, and once you take it, the next instruction comes. One who relies on the Spirit with the heart takes a step and listens for the next; one who relies on himself with the head insists on seeing the whole map before moving, and often misses that chariot.

His first words were not a sermon but a question: “Do you understand what you are reading?” He first listened to what the other was reading, then asked, then waited for the other to invite him up. And the passage the eunuch was reading was Isaiah 53—the clearest picture of the suffering servant in the Old Testament: like a lamb before its shearers, silent, not opening his mouth, taken away, humbled to the end. The eunuch asked, “Of whom does the prophet say this?” In verse 35: “Philip opened his mouth, and beginning from this Scripture, preached to him Jesus.”

Beginning from this Scripture—Philip did not begin from his own experience, not from the miracles in Samaria, but from the scroll in the eunuch’s hands, and preached Jesus. And that Lamb who “opened not his mouth” is the very example of self-denial—He had all authority, yet was silent before His shearers.
• One turn at a time: the Spirit’s guidance is step by step, not the full map first.
• Begin from that Scripture: first listen to what people are reading, then preach Jesus from there, not starting from yourself.
IV. “Behold, here is water”—Nothing Hinders

Verses 36 to 38: “As they went on the way, they came to a certain water, and the eunuch said, ‘Behold, here is water. What prevents me from being baptized?’… He commanded the chariot to stand still, and they both went down into the water, both Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him.”

“What prevents me?”—this sentence from a eunuch’s mouth carries special weight. All his life he had been “prevented”: unable to enter the temple, join the assembly, or leave descendants. Now he asks: if I am baptized, is anything still in the way? Philip’s answer was action—the chariot stood still, and both went down into the water. Nothing hindered. In Christ, the law that shut him outside was torn down by the cross.

The eunuch himself “commanded the chariot to stand still.” This man in charge of a nation’s treasury stopped his chariot by a wilderness roadside and let a stranger, a Jew, baptize him. This is a man of power laying down power and returning to his place—what humility looks like in him is: not waiting for a more dignified occasion; where there is water, go down into it.
• Nothing hinders: the cross tore down the wall that shut people out.
• Where there is water, go down: the humble don’t wait for a dignified occasion but obey on the spot.
V. “The Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away… he went on his way rejoicing”—Each on His Own Road

Verses 39 and 40: “When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away, and the eunuch didn’t see him any more, for he went on his way rejoicing. But Philip was found at Azotus. Passing through, he preached the Good News to all the cities, until he came to Caesarea.”

Philip was suddenly taken away, and the eunuch “didn’t see him any more.” Luke does not write that he panicked or searched everywhere, only that he “went on his way rejoicing.” His joy was not tied to Philip but to the One he believed in. The preacher can go; the Lord does not. And Philip turned up in Azotus, preaching city by city until Caesarea—years later, Paul stayed in that city at the house of “Philip the evangelist” (Acts 21:8).

One went south to the ends of the earth, the other north to take root in the coastal cities. God let two men meet for an hour on a wilderness road, then sent each on his own way. This encounter built no organization; it was only one person pointing another to Jesus, and then letting go.
• Joy isn’t tied to a person: the preacher can be taken away; the Lord will not be.
• Meet for an hour, affect a lifetime: point people to Jesus, then let go—that is enough.
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Spirit’s Guidance, Scripture’s Standard, Jesus’ Example—All in One Chariot
This passage lays out all three foundations at once.

The Holy Spirit is my guide: the angel said “go south,” the Spirit said “go near the chariot,” and finally “the Spirit of the Lord caught Philip away”—not one step was arranged by Philip himself. The Bible is my standard: he “began from this Scripture” to preach Jesus, not starting from experience. Jesus is my example: what the eunuch was reading was precisely that Servant who, like a lamb, did not open His mouth—the prototype of self-denial.

And the purpose of all this was to bring a man shut outside inside, to go on his way rejoicing. Building God’s system is often not in a city but on a wilderness road, for one person. A person of self-denial is willing to leave the crowd for an empty road, because his focus is not on the scene but on the one the Lord wants him to meet.
a: Arise and Go
If the Lord’s sending gives no reason, obey first; the reason comes on the road.
See the One Outside the Door
Notice the person near you who fears God yet feels shut outside.
One Step, Then Listen
Don’t demand the whole map first; the Spirit gives only the next turn.
Begin from That Scripture
Speak of Jesus beginning from the Bible, not from your own experience.
Let Go, Don’t Grasp
After pointing someone to Jesus, allow yourself to be “taken away”; don’t keep people attached to yourself.
q: Is there something now where the Lord has already said “Arise and go” to you, and you are still waiting for Him to give a reason first? What would it look like if today you “arose and went”?
Think of someone near you who fears God yet feels he “cannot enter the temple.” What is he reading, and what is he asking? How could you “go near that chariot”?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that for one man shut outside the temple door, You sent a preacher away from a whole city in revival to a road in the wilderness. Thank You that Your temple has a threshold, but Your heaven has none; You had already said to that eunuch in Isaiah: you are not a dry tree.
Lord Jesus, You are that Servant who like a lamb did not open His mouth, our example of self-denial. Give us Philip’s obedience: when You say arise, we arise; when You say go near the chariot, we run. Teach us to begin from Scripture and point people to You, not begin from ourselves or keep people for ourselves. And open our eyes to see the one near us who is seeking You yet feels shut outside, and give us courage to walk up to his chariot and ask: Do you understand what you are reading? In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: But Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest
and asked for letters from him to the synagogues of Damascus, that if he found any who were of the Way, whether men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
As he traveled, he got close to Damascus, and suddenly a light from the sky shone around him.
He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”
He said, “Who are you, Lord?” The Lord said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
But rise up and enter into the city, then you will be told what you must do.”
The men who traveled with him stood speechless, hearing the sound, but seeing no one.
Saul arose from the ground, and when his eyes were opened, he saw no one. They led him by the hand, and brought him into Damascus.
He was without sight for three days, and neither ate nor drank.
b: In the last devotion, the eunuch went south rejoicing, and Philip preached the gospel from town to town along the coast. The road of the gospel toward the ends of the earth seemed to be growing wider and wider.

But Luke turns the camera back to the name we met at the beginning of chapter 8. Saul is on the road too—on his way to Damascus, with arrest papers in his hand. Chapter 8 showed the gospel spreading because it was scattered; chapter 9 shows the persecutor of the gospel being struck down himself. This is the most famous conversion in church history, and its central action is just one: a man who was standing falls to the ground.
I. “Still breathing threats and slaughter”—A Man Who Breathed Persecution

Verses 1–2: “But Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest, and asked for letters from him to the synagogues of Damascus, that if he found any who were of the Way, whether men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.”

“Still”—from chapter 8 until now, he has not stopped. “Breathing” is literally the word for respiration: threats and slaughter had become the very air he drew in and let out. Jerusalem was not enough for him; he went to the high priest on his own initiative to ask for papers so he could pursue them as far as Damascus. Damascus lies more than 130 miles north of Jerusalem, about a week’s journey on foot, and the city had many Jews and synagogues. He meant to bring the disciples who had fled there “bound to Jerusalem,” men and women alike.

Here Luke for the first time calls believers by the name “the Way”—“any who were of the Way.” Believing in Jesus is not joining an organization; it is setting out on a road. And the road Saul was walking was another one: a road of serving God by his own zeal, his own righteousness, his own papers. This is what zeal full of self looks like at its extreme: so certain of being right that people can be bound. What this looks like today is that the more sure I am that I am acting for God, the more I should watch whether I am holding a set of papers meant to “bind” someone.
• Zeal can take the wrong road: Saul did not lack zeal; he lacked direction.
• Watch the papers in your hand: the more certain you are that you are right, the more you should ask, “Whom am I about to bind?”
II. “Suddenly a light from heaven shone around him… he fell to the ground”—The Standing Man Went Down
Verses 3–4a: “As he traveled, it happened that he got close to Damascus, and suddenly a light from the sky shone around him. He fell on the earth.”

“Got close”—the destination was right in front of him, the papers were in hand, the plan was complete, victory was in sight. And then, “suddenly.” Paul later said it was “about noon” (Acts 22:6)—under the midday sun, there was a light brighter than the sun “shining around him.” He did not choose to kneel; he “fell”—he was struck down.

This is the first movement of a life being turned over, and a necessary one. Saul had been standing the whole way: standing beside the coats at Stephen’s stoning, standing at people’s doorways, standing before the high priest. A man who stands and seizes others must first go down before he can hear. Pride is leaving one’s place and putting oneself where one does not belong; God’s first step with pride is often not to argue but to lay a person low. What this looks like today: those moments when I “cannot stand”—a plan suddenly torn apart, a body suddenly laid low, confidence suddenly collapsing—may very well not be an attack but light.
• When the light came, the man was down: the Lord did not debate with Saul; He laid him low.
• A moment when you cannot stand may be light: do not hurry to get up; listen first.
III. “Why are you persecuting me?”—The Lord and His People Are One
Verses 4b–5: “And he heard a voice saying to him, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’ He said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ The Lord said, ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.’”

“Saul, Saul!”—calling a name twice is how God calls people in Scripture: “Abraham! Abraham!” “Moses! Moses!” “Samuel! Samuel!” This is not the tone of judgment but the tone of calling. Then comes a question: “Why do you persecute me?” Notice: not “persecute them,” but “persecute me.” Saul was seizing disciples; the Lord said, you are seizing Me. He is in heaven and His people are on earth, yet He says they are one—to touch them is to touch Me.

Saul asked, “Who are you, Lord?” This is the most honest sentence in the whole passage. All his life he had thought he knew God and was zealous for God, yet only at this moment did he learn that he did not know the One speaking to him. The answer: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.” The crucified Nazarene, said to have risen, was the very God he thought he was serving. The whole direction of his zeal was wrong.
• To touch the church is to touch Him: the Lord and His people are one—the starting point of all Paul’s later teaching on the body of Christ.
• “Who are you?” is the starting point: a person who has been zealous for God for half a lifetime may still not truly know Him.
IV. “Rise up, and enter into the city, and it will be told you”—The Man With Papers Must Be Told
Verses 6–7: “But rise up, and enter into the city, and it will be told you what you must do.” The men who traveled with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one.

The Lord did not finish telling everything on the road; He gave only the next step: get up, enter the city, someone will tell you. This is a great reversal: Saul was the man with papers who was going to “tell” the synagogues what to do; now the Lord says what you must do “will be told you.” From the one who gave orders to the one who waits for instructions; from the one holding papers to the one waiting for word.

Humility is laying down power and returning to one’s place. What it looks like in Saul: he is no longer the one deciding other people’s fate; he must wait for someone to tell him even his own next step. And the one who tells him will be one of the very disciples he came to seize.
• From telling to being told: the Lord took him from the seat of command and put him back in the place of obedience.
• One step at a time: get up, enter, wait—this is how the Lord’s guidance always goes.
V. “Led him by the hand… three days without sight”—Three Days of Being Led

Verses 8–9: “Saul arose from the ground, and when his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. They led him by the hand, and brought him into Damascus. He was without sight for three days, and neither ate nor drank.”

He stood up, but he could not see. The one who came to bind people was now led by the hand into the city; the one who meant to lead people back to Jerusalem was now led into Damascus. Three days, blind, neither eating nor drinking.

These three days are blank. Luke does not write what he thought, but we can imagine: the whole foundation of his life collapsed—what he was sure of was wrong, and the one he persecuted was the Lord. These three days were not punishment but emptying. A phone must be shut down before the system can update; while the old is still running, the new cannot be installed. Saul’s old self was shut down during these three days—not seeing, not eating, not drinking, not doing—so that God could install a completely new man. Self-denial is not nothing; it is entering the limitless. But before that, there must be days of having nothing at all.
• Being led: from controller to the one led—this is the first posture of new life.
• Blank means emptying, not punishment: the old is shut down so the new can be installed.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Pride Falls, Self-Denial Begins
These nine verses are the story of a man full of self being laid low.

Saul is the old self at its peak: zealous, certain, authorized, with papers in hand and strong drive to act—everything good, except one thing wrong: the center of that zeal was his own righteousness. A person full of self is not necessarily wicked; he may be extremely devout. He is simply standing in a place that does not belong to him, deciding who is right and who must be bound. Pride is leaving one’s place, and Saul had gone very far.

The Lord dealt with him not by persuading but by light; not by giving him more but by emptying him: falling down, blindness, being led by the hand, three days without eating or drinking. This is the starting point of self-denial—not that he decided to lay down himself, but that he was laid down, and then in the blankness asked for the first time, “Who are you, Lord?”

Change begins with “Who are you?” A person who has never truly been laid low may well be zealous all his life for a god of his own imagining. And God gives grace to the humble: those three days of darkness were the beginning of the greatest grace of this man’s life.
a: Check the Direction of Your Zeal
The more sure I am that I act for God, the more I should ask whether I hold papers to bind someone.
Don’t Rush to Get Up
A moment when I cannot stand may be light; listen first to what He says.
See the Oneness
How I treat my brothers and sisters, the Lord says, “is how you treat Me.”
From Giving Orders to Receiving Them
Let the Lord move me from the place of telling to the place of being told.
Allow a Blank Space
The old must be shut down before the new can be installed; do not fear those three days.
q: Recall an experience of being “laid low” in your life—a plan collapsing, a body failing, confidence shattering. Looking back now, was it an attack or light? Did you hear Him call your name there?
“I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.” Is there a brother or sister whom you have recently treated in a way that you would need to look at again if the Lord said, “That is how you treat Me”?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You did not give up even on a man who breathed persecution. He went toward Damascus with papers in hand, and You waited for him on the road; he stood, and You laid him down; he could not see, and You took his hand. Thank You that Your way with pride is light, and that You give grace to those who fall.
Lord Jesus, we confess that there is a Saul in us too: certain that we are right and that our zeal is for You, yet often standing where we do not belong, deciding who should be bound. Shine on us. If the direction of our zeal is wrong, lay us low, and do not let us travel all the way to Damascus. Teach us, in the moments when we cannot stand, not to hurry to get up, but first to ask, “Who are You, Lord?” Give us also a blank three days, to shut down the old and install You Yourself, so that we no longer live for ourselves, but You live in us. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Now there was a certain disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias!” He said, “Behold, it’s me, Lord.”
The Lord said to him, “Arise, and go to the street which is called Straight, and inquire in the house of Judah for one named Saul, a man of Tarsus. For behold, he is praying,
and in a vision he has seen a man named Ananias coming in and laying his hands on him, that he might receive his sight.”
But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he did to your saints at Jerusalem.
Here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.”
But the Lord said to him, “Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel.
For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake.”

Ananias departed and entered into the house. Laying his hands on him, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord, who appeared to you on the road by which you came, has sent me that you may receive your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”
Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He arose and was baptized.
He took food and was strengthened. Saul stayed several days with the disciples who were at Damascus.
b: In the last devotion, Saul fell on the road to Damascus, was led by the hand into the city, and for three days could not see, neither eating nor drinking. The Lord had said to him, “It will be told you what you must do.”

Who was that “someone”? There was a disciple in Damascus named Ananias. He was not an apostle or a deacon; Scripture mentions him only in these few verses. Yet the great vessel the Lord had chosen would open his eyes through these ordinary hands. This is the gentlest scene in Acts: a frightened disciple walks into his enemy’s room and calls him “brother.”
I. “Behold, here I am, Lord”—An Ordinary Disciple’s Answer
Verse 10: “Now there was a certain disciple at Damascus, named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, ‘Ananias!’ He said, ‘Behold, it’s I, Lord.’”

Paul later described him as “a devout man according to the law, well reported of by all the Jews who lived there” (Acts 22:12)—a quiet, law-abiding believer of good reputation. When the Lord called his name, he gave the most classic answer in the Old Testament: “Here I am, Lord.” Samuel answered this way, and Isaiah did too. It does not mean “I am ready”; it means “I am here; You speak.”

First God, then oneself, then people, then tasks—Ananias had the order right. He first stood before the Lord and said “Here I am,” and only then heard what the matter was. Often our order is reversed: we first listen to what we are asked to do, then decide whether to be present. What this looks like today: before looking at the day’s schedule in the morning, say to the Lord, “Here I am.”
• Be present first, then listen: obedience does not begin with agreeing to the task but with placing oneself before the Lord.
• Ordinary disciples are called by name too: the Lord’s great work often passes through unknown hands.
II. “Go to the street called Straight… behold, he is praying”—The Lord Was Already at Work on Both Sides

Verses 11–12: “Arise, and go to the street which is called Straight, and inquire in the house of Judas for one named Saul, a man of Tarsus. For behold, he is praying, and in a vision he has seen a man named Ananias coming in, and laying his hands on him, that he might receive his sight.”

The Lord’s instructions were extremely specific: which street (Straight Street, a road still found in Damascus today), whose house, what kind of man, from where. Then three words: “he is praying.” The man who breathed threats and slaughter was now praying. And the Lord had already shown Saul in a vision a man named Ananias coming in to lay hands on him. That is, before Ananias even left home, the Lord had already told Saul his name on the other side of the room.

This is the most reassuring part of the Holy Spirit’s guidance: He does not only send me; He prepares the other side at the same time. I think I am going to find that person, but that person is already waiting for me. Those who rely wholeheartedly on the Holy Spirit know that on the road of obedience the Lord is at both ends.
• The Lord works on both sides: before I go out, the other person is already waiting.
• “He is praying”: the person you fear most may be kneeling before the Lord.
III. “Lord, I have heard from many”—Honest Fear

Verses 13–14: “But Ananias answered, ‘Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he did to your saints at Jerusalem. Here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.’”

Ananias did not immediately say, “Yes, I’ll go.” He first told the Lord honestly the fear in his heart: I have heard about this man; he did evil to Your saints in Jerusalem; he came here to bind people like us. This is not disobedience; it is honesty. He knew Saul’s reputation and knew he might not come back.

The Lord did not rebuke his fear. In Scripture obedience is rarely without struggle; Moses struggled, Jeremiah struggled, and the Lord Himself struggled in Gethsemane. Bringing the struggle before the Lord is closer to real faith than hiding it and pretending to obey.
• Fear can be spoken: the Lord does not want pretended bravery but honest obedience.
• Struggle is not unbelief: hand “I have heard from many” to the Lord, and He answers with “Just go.”
IV. “He is my chosen vessel”—Vessel and Suffering

Verses 15–16: “But the Lord said to him, ‘Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel. For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake.’”

The Lord’s answer did not deny Ananias’ information; it simply gave him another viewpoint—God’s. You see a man who harmed the saints; I see “my chosen vessel.” This man will bear My name before the nations, kings, and the children of Israel—this one sentence is the outline of the next nineteen chapters of Acts.

The word “vessel” speaks of a container: a jar, a bowl, a pot. A vessel has one characteristic: its value is not in itself but in what it holds; and it can hold something because it is empty inside. A clay jar stuffed full of itself can hold nothing. Saul had been emptied in those three days—not seeing, not eating, not drinking—and now the Lord says: this is My vessel. Self-denial is not nothing but entering the limitless; this is exactly what it means: emptied of self, we can hold all that God wants to put in.

Then comes verse 16, a line many dare not read: “how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake.” Choosing and suffering come together. This man once made others suffer; now he will suffer for the Lord’s name. To be chosen is not to be lifted up but to be entrusted with a road.
• A vessel’s value is in being empty: God cannot fill a person who is stuffed full of himself.
• Choosing and suffering come together: being chosen is not being exalted but being entrusted with a road to walk.
V. “Brother Saul”—A Pair of Hands Laid On

Verses 17–19: “Ananias departed, and entered into the house. Laying his hands on him, he said, ‘Brother Saul, the Lord, who appeared to you on the way which you came, has sent me, that you may receive your sight, and be filled with the Holy Spirit.’ Immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he received his sight. He arose and was baptized. He took food and was strengthened. Saul stayed several days with the disciples who were at Damascus.”

“Ananias departed.” When the fear had been spoken, he went. Once inside, the first thing he did was lay his hands on that man—on the hands that had come to bind him; the first thing he said was “Brother Saul.” This was the first address Saul heard from the church after his conversion. Not “you persecutor,” not “what are you doing here,” but “brother.” What self-denial looks like in Ananias is these two words: he laid down his own fear, his own rights, his own position, and what remained was only how the Lord sees this man.

Then the scales fell, his eyes opened, he was baptized, he ate and was strengthened, and “stayed several days with the disciples who were at Damascus.” The man who came to bind the disciples now lived with them. A pair of ordinary hands led an enemy into the family.
• “Departed”: when the fear is spoken, go—this is honest obedience.
• The first word was “brother”: what new life needs most is someone who first calls him brother.
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Vessel Emptied of Self and the Hands Emptied of Self
This passage has two people emptied of self.

Saul was the vessel that was emptied. For three days he did not see, eat, or drink; everything he had relied on all his life was taken away, and then the Lord said: this is My chosen vessel. A vessel’s use is in its emptiness—no longer I, but Christ; not I who live, but Christ living in me. That this man could later write that sentence is because, in that room on Straight Street, he was first emptied.

Ananias was the hand emptied of self. He was not without fear; after he had spoken his fear, he still chose to let the Lord be King—the Lord said go, and he went. He put his own safety second and the Lord’s heart toward this man first, walked in, laid on hands, and called him brother.

This is how God’s system is built: not by one great person but by an emptied vessel and a pair of willing hands. People matter more than tasks—Ananias’ trip accomplished no “ministry” at all; he only received a person. Yet the second half of Acts begins from that one act of receiving.
a: Say “Here I Am” First
Before hearing what the matter is, place yourself before the Lord.
Believe the Lord Works on Both Sides
Before I go out, the other person has already been prepared.
Speak Your Fear Honestly
The Lord does not want pretended bravery; hand Him your “I have heard.”
Let Yourself Be Emptied
A vessel’s value is in being empty; what has stuffed me full today so that God cannot fill me?
Call Him “Brother” First
To the one who once hurt me, let the Lord’s eyes replace my position.
q: When the Lord calls your name, is your first reaction “Here I am,” or “Let me see what it is first”? This morning, are you willing to say the first one?
Is there someone whom you know only through “I have heard from many”? The Lord’s view of this person may differ from what you have heard. Are you willing to walk in and first call him brother?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Your great work passes through ordinary hands. Thank You for choosing an unknown disciple to walk into his enemy’s room and call him brother; and thank You that You work on both sides of the room at once, letting the man who breathed threats first kneel in prayer.
Lord Jesus, we confess that we often listen first to what the matter is before deciding whether to be “here”; we also often hide our fear and pretend to obey without really going. Teach us to be like Ananias, to say first “Here I am, Lord,” then honestly speak our fear, and then go. Empty us, make us vessels in Your hands, no longer stuffed with ourselves, so that You can fill us. And show us who the “Saul” in our lives is—the one we fear most and least want to receive—and give us hands willing to lay on and a word willing to say, “Brother.” In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Immediately in the synagogues he proclaimed the Christ, that he is the Son of God.
All who heard him were amazed, and said, “Isn’t this he who in Jerusalem made havoc of those who called on this name? And he had come here intending to bring them bound before the chief priests!”
But Saul increased more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived at Damascus, proving that this is the Christ.
When many days were fulfilled, the Jews conspired together to kill him,
but their plot became known to Saul. They watched the gates both day and night that they might kill him,
but his disciples took him by night and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket.
b: In the last devotion, Ananias walked into the house on Straight Street, laid his hands on Saul, and called him “brother.” The scales fell, his eyes opened, he was baptized, ate, and stayed several days with the disciples in Damascus.

And then? What is the first thing a man who was just breathing threats does after believing? Luke connects it with a single word: “immediately.” These six verses record Saul’s first stop in preaching and also the first time he was hunted down. The man who entered the city with papers finally left it in a basket.
I. “Immediately in the synagogues he proclaimed Jesus, that he is the Son of God”—Papers Became a Sermon
Verse 20: “Immediately in the synagogues he proclaimed the Christ, that he is the Son of God.”

Remember why he had come: “letters… to the synagogues of Damascus” (9:2). Those synagogues were where he meant to hunt the disciples; now he stood in the same synagogues, and what he proclaimed was not papers but Jesus. “Proclaimed” in the original means “to announce publicly like a herald”—he was not sharing privately; he stood up in public.

His content also deserves notice: “that he is the Son of God.” In the whole book of Acts, only here is “Son of God” the theme of a sermon. Peter preached “Lord, Christ,” Stephen spoke of “the Son of Man,” and Saul’s very first words were “Son of God.” This is exactly what he saw on the road: that light brighter than the noonday sun, and the One who said “I am Jesus,” could only be the Son of God. A person preaches the One he has truly seen.
• Papers became a sermon: the Lord did not merely stop a persecutor; He took over his whole route.
• Preach what you have truly seen: the content of Saul’s first sermon was the One he met on the road.
II. “All who heard him were amazed”—The Most Powerful Sermon Is a Changed Person

Verse 21: “All who heard him were amazed, and said, ‘Isn’t this he who in Jerusalem made havoc of those who called on this name? And he had come here intending to bring them bound before the chief priests.’”

The word “made havoc” here is stronger than the “laid waste the church” of chapter 8; it means “to destroy, to raze”—Paul himself later used this same word to describe his former self (Gal. 1:13). The people of Damascus knew who he was and why he came. So what amazed them was not only his teaching but the man teaching. Not one sentence of theirs refuted his content; all of it spoke of his past: “Isn’t this the man?”

This is where testimony is most powerful. Doctrine can be argued; a changed person cannot. Change the concept and you change life; change life and you change living—Saul’s concept was overturned on the road, his life was emptied and reinstalled on Straight Street, and his living changed along with it: from one who bound people to one who proclaimed Jesus. Those around him did not need to hear a whole sermon; just seeing the man amazed them. What this looks like today: when the people around me see me, is there any bit of “isn’t this the one?” amazement?
• A changed person cannot be argued with: the most powerful sermon is the person standing there.
• What amazes people is not eloquence: it is the gap of “isn’t this the man?”
III. “Increased more in strength… proving that this is the Christ”—Where Power Comes From
Verse 22: “But Saul increased more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived at Damascus, proving that this is the Christ.”

“Increased more in strength”—he was not strong from the start; he grew stronger as he went. “Confounded” in the original means “to throw into confusion, to leave speechless”; “proving” means “to put things together”—he assembled the Old Testament passages piece by piece so people could see that these Scriptures pointed to Jesus. These were the scrolls he had read from childhood under Gamaliel; once he used them against Jesus, and now the same Scriptures were pieced together by him into the image of Jesus. The Bible is my standard—the standard did not change; the reader got new eyes.

“After many days were fulfilled” (verse 23)—these words hide a long stretch of time. Paul himself says that after his conversion he “went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus. Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem” (Gal. 1:17–18). So these “many days” may be as long as three years, during which he withdrew to the desert of Arabia. A person grows in strength often not because he becomes busier and busier, but because in between there is a stretch of quiet days in which he reads the standard through and reads himself empty.
• The same Bible with new eyes: once used against the Lord, now used to prove the Lord.
• Power comes “more and more”: those wilderness days in between are the source of power.
IV. “They watched the gates both day and night that they might kill him”—The Persecutor Persecuted
Verses 23–24: “When many days were fulfilled, the Jews conspired together to kill him, but their plot became known to Saul. They watched the gates both day and night that they might kill him.”

The roles were reversed. A few years earlier he came with papers to bind people; now he was the one being watched to be killed. Day and night people kept watch at the gates, ready to strike the moment he stepped out. Paul later added a detail: the governor under King Aretas also guarded the city gates (2 Cor. 11:32)—even the local government was drawn in.

The Lord had long ago said to Ananias, “how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake” (9:16). This was the first. Saul did not complain, and Luke does not write that he was surprised. A person who understands that choosing and suffering come together will not treat persecution as an accident. The focus is on Jesus, not on circumstances—circumstances went from “the man with papers” to “the man being watched,” but the Name on his lips did not change.
• Roles may reverse: once binding people, now being watched; those who follow the Lord must be mentally prepared.
• Suffering is not an accident: the Lord already said “must,” so when it comes you do not feel deceived.
V. “Let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket”—A Great Man’s Little Basket
Verse 25: “But his disciples took him by night, and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a basket.”

“His disciples”—he already had a group following him. They put him in a basket by night and lowered him down the city wall. Picture the scene: a rabbi with the highest education, a man who once carried the high priest’s papers, now curled up in a cargo basket, lowered bit by bit on a rope.

This basket Paul never forgot in his whole life. Years later he wrote in 2 Corinthians, “If I must boast, I will boast of the things that concern my weakness.” And the first thing he told was this basket (2 Cor. 11:30–33). This was the first entry on his “résumé”—not how many people he had refuted, but being put in a basket to escape.

A person full of self wants to remember only how he looked standing on the platform; a person emptied of self does not mind remembering how he looked curled in a basket, because he knows that at that moment it was the Lord’s hand letting out the rope. What humility looks like in Paul: he took the most humiliating scene of his life as the most worthy thing to boast of.
• A great man’s little basket: the Lord used a cargo basket to teach a rabbi what weakness means.
• Boast in weakness: keep the most humiliating scene, because it was the Lord’s hand letting out the rope.
The Light of the 321 Principles: A Changed Person Is the Witness
In these six verses, what amazes most is not the preaching but the preacher.

The people of Damascus did not need anyone to prove to them that the gospel has power—they saw with their own eyes the one who came to bind people now proclaiming Jesus in the synagogue. Change begins with me—for Saul this was no slogan: he did not first go and change the Jews of Damascus; he was changed himself first, and the people around him were amazed.

And the evidence of this change is not only in the side of him that grew in power, but also in the side of him that was put in a basket. A person who truly lets Jesus be King is the same person on the platform and off: when standing and preaching, he gives glory to the Lord; when curled in a basket, he also knows it is the Lord letting out the rope. When the focus is not on self, one does not fear looking ugly.

Let Jesus have all the glory, including the glory of my most humiliating scene. Paul later said, “When I am weak, then am I strong” (2 Cor. 12:10), and the first lesson of that sentence was the basket on the wall of Damascus.
a: Let the Papers Become a Sermon
The Lord can take over the route I meant to travel and replace the whole of what I was going to do.
Let Yourself Be the Witness
When the people around me see me, is there any bit of “isn’t this the one?” amazement?
Give Yourself a Wilderness
Power comes “more and more”; do not skip those quiet days of reading the standard through.
Don’t Treat Suffering as an Accident
The Lord has said “must”; when it comes, you will not feel deceived.
Remember Your Basket
Keep the most humiliating scene as a memorial of the Lord’s hand letting out the rope.
q: If the people of Damascus saw you today, would they say “Isn’t this the man?” What gap in your life can others see?
Have you had a “basket” experience—humiliating, running away, nothing looking dignified? Paul put it first among his boasts. Are you willing to see it again as the moment the Lord let out the rope?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You did not merely stop a persecutor but took over his whole route: the synagogues he meant to raid became the platform from which he proclaimed Jesus. Thank You for letting the people of Damascus see that a changed person is the most powerful sermon.
Lord Jesus, we confess that we often want to change others first and are unwilling to let You change us first; we also want to remember only how we looked on the platform and not how we looked curled in a basket. Make us witnesses who amaze people, not because of eloquence but because of the gap. Give us a stretch of quiet days to read Your word through and read ourselves empty, so that our power comes “more and more.” And teach us, like Paul, to take our weakest scene as the most worthy thing to boast of, because it was Your hand letting out the rope. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: When Saul had come to Jerusalem, he tried to join himself to the disciples; but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple.

But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles, and declared to them how he had seen the Lord on the way, and that he had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.
He was with them entering into Jerusalem,
preaching boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus. He spoke and disputed against the Hellenists, but they were seeking to kill him.
When the brothers knew it, they brought him down to Caesarea, and sent him off to Tarsus.
So the assemblies throughout all Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace, and were built up. They were multiplied, walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit.
b: In the last devotion, Saul was put in a basket and lowered down the wall of Damascus. That was the first suffering he bore for the Lord’s name, and also the scene he later most willingly “boasted” of.

After the basket touched the ground, where did he go? Jerusalem—the city where he once broke into house after house to seize people. This time he came back not with papers but wanting to “join himself to the disciples.” But the disciples were afraid of him. These six verses tell how a man was kept outside the door by his own past, and how one person’s acceptance brought him in.
I. “They were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple”—Kept Outside by His Own Past
Verse 26: “When he had come to Jerusalem, he tried to join himself to the disciples; but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple.”

By Paul’s own account, this was three years after his conversion (Gal. 1:18). For three years the people of Damascus had known he had changed, but the disciples in Jerusalem had not. What they remembered was the Saul who “laid waste the church, entering into every house, and dragging both men and women, committed them to prison.” Those he took away three years earlier may have been these people’s own family. “Not believing that he was a disciple”—they even suspected he might be an infiltrator.

This is a situation a new believer often faces: the Lord has forgiven, but people have not yet; the Lord looks at today, people remember the past. Saul did not argue about it, nor did he turn around and leave. A person truly changed by the Lord can bear that others are still afraid—because he knows that the fear is something he caused. What humility looks like here: do not demand that people immediately believe I have changed; give them time.
• The Lord has forgiven, people may not yet: new life needs the patience to bear others’ hesitation.
• Neither argue nor leave: let time and life speak.
II. “But Barnabas took him”—One Person’s Acceptance

Verse 27: “But Barnabas took him, and brought him to the apostles, and declared to them how he had seen the Lord on the way, and that he had spoken to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.”

“But”—everyone was afraid; only one person reached out a hand. We met this man in chapter 4: Joseph, who sold his field and laid the money at the apostles’ feet, called “son of encouragement.” “Took” in the original means “to grasp, to lay hold of”—not a nod of acknowledgment, but reaching out and taking hold of him, bringing him before the apostles. Barnabas told them three things: how he saw the Lord on the road, how the Lord spoke to him, how he preached boldly in Damascus. He first took time to listen to Saul’s story, and only then testified for him.

Think of a new hire with a bad reputation. Everyone avoids him, until one senior colleague walks over at lunch and sits beside him. That meal does more good than any letter of recommendation. This is what Barnabas did: he staked his standing in the church on a man everyone feared. People matter more than tasks, relationships more than things—Barnabas did no “ministry” that day; he only received one person. But without that day, there would have been no Paul afterward.
• “But” one person is enough: the whole church need not accept him; first someone reaches out a hand.
• Stake your own reputation: accepting a person is putting your name on him.
III. “Going in and going out… preaching boldly… disputing”—Standing Where Stephen Stood
Verses 28–29: “He was with them entering into Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. He spoke and disputed against the Hellenists, but they were seeking to kill him.”

“Going in and going out”—he became one of the disciples and lived with them. Then he went to a certain place to preach: among “the Hellenists.” Remember who they were. In chapter 6, it was these Hellenist Jews who disputed with Stephen, could not withstand him, then suborned false witnesses and sent him to be stoned (Acts 6:9–14); and Saul stood by guarding the coats. Three years later, Saul stood in the place where Stephen had stood, speaking of the same Lord to the same people, and the result was the same: “they were seeking to kill him.”

This scene has a sacred answer in it. At the place where Stephen fell, he had once kept people’s coats; now he himself stepped into that place. God did not waste Stephen’s blood; He used the very man who guarded the coats to take up Stephen’s position. What self-sacrifice looks like here: knowing that to stand there would mean being hunted, he stood there anyway.
• Taking up for the one who fell: God used a keeper of coats to take the martyr’s place.
• Standing though it costs: self-sacrifice is not passive suffering but actively standing where one should stand.
IV. “Brought him down to Caesarea, and sent him off to Tarsus”—The Silent Years at Home
Verse 30: “When the brothers knew it, they brought him down to Caesarea, and sent him off to Tarsus.”

Sent away again. In Damascus the disciples lowered him in a basket; in Jerusalem the brothers sent him off by ship—from the port at Caesarea back to his hometown of Tarsus. Paul later said that the Lord spoke to him in the temple: “Hurry and get out of Jerusalem quickly… I will send you far from here to the Gentiles” (Acts 22:17–21). He wanted to stay in Jerusalem to testify, but the Lord told him to go.

Then came a long silence. From this verse to chapter 11, when Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for him (Acts 11:25), was about ten years. In these ten years Luke wrote not a word. The one “chosen vessel” was in his hometown doing things nobody recorded. A person full of self cannot bear this silence: I clearly have ability and calling; why am I set aside? A person emptied of self knows that being set aside is also the Lord’s arrangement—waiting is not waste but the Lord preparing a greater harvest field.
• Sent away twice: the protection of disciples and brothers was also the Lord’s guidance.
• Ten years of silence: the days of being set aside are the Lord preparing a person for a greater field.
V. “The church throughout all Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace, and was built up”—A Summary

Verse 31: “So the assemblies throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace, and were built up. They were walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, and were multiplied.”

This is Luke’s summary of the first stage of Acts. Notice that “church” is singular: Judea, Galilee, Samaria—three regions, one church. The delay of the Holy Spirit in chapter 8 was for exactly this: Samaria and Judea are one family. And the “peace” was partly because the fiercest persecutor was now a brother.

Luke gives this church four descriptions: peace, being built up, the fear of the Lord, the comfort of the Holy Spirit—and only then “multiplied.” Multiplying is the result, not the goal. First life (fear of the Lord), then relationships (peace, being built up), then ministry (multiplying). “Fear of the Lord” and “comfort of the Holy Spirit” stand side by side: one is the standard, one is the guidance; one keeps people from being careless, the other keeps people from being afraid.
• One church, three regions: the delay in chapter 8, and in chapter 9 the fruit is seen.
• Multiplying is the result: fear the Lord, receive comfort, be built up, and the numbers come by themselves.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry
Verse 31 states the whole order.

The church “had peace, and was built up”—this is relationships; “walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit”—this is life; “were multiplied”—this is ministry. Luke puts “multiplied” last, and joins it with “and”: when what comes before is right, what comes after follows. We often do it backward: chase numbers first, patch relationships after, and think of life last; the numbers come, but there is no peace inside.

And the most visible “relationship” in this passage is the hand Barnabas reached out. Saul had life and also power, but without one person receiving him, he could not enter that system. Building God’s system is not a gifted person forcing his way in, but a person emptied of self first reaching out a hand to pull him in.

Barnabas kept nothing for himself—he staked his reputation, brought Saul to the apostles, and then stepped back. Years later “Barnabas and Saul” would become “Paul and Barnabas,” and he did not mind that either. This is self-denial: for Jesus, for others, not for self, and then watching the church have peace and be built up.
a: Bear Others’ Hesitation
The Lord has forgiven me, but people may need time; do not argue, let life speak.
Be the “But”
Is there someone in the church everyone avoids? First reach out and take hold of him.
Stand Where You Should Stand
Though it costs, stand in the place where Stephen stood.
Accept the Silent Years
Being set aside is not being forgotten; the Lord is preparing a greater field.
Follow the Order
First fear the Lord, receive comfort, be built up, and the numbers will multiply by themselves.
q: Is there someone around you whom everyone avoids because of his “past”? Are you willing to be the “but,” and walk over and sit beside him?
Are you now in a stretch of “Tarsus years”—with calling and ability, yet set aside? What might the Lord be preparing for you in these days?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You used a keeper of coats to take up Stephen’s place; and You used the hand of a son of encouragement to pull in Saul, whom everyone feared, into Your house. Thank You that Judea, Galilee, and Samaria became one church, having peace and being built up.
Lord Jesus, we confess that we often remember others’ past more than we believe what You are doing in them today; we also often chase numbers first and put life and relationships behind. Give us the heart of Barnabas, willing to stake our reputation on a rejected person; give us also the heart of Saul, who stood where he should though it cost; and give us rest in the silent years, knowing that being set aside is not being forgotten. Make our church fear You in all things and receive the comfort of the Holy Spirit, so that growth in numbers is the fruit of life and not a goal we chase. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: As Peter went throughout all those parts, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda.
There he found a certain man named Aeneas, who had been bedridden for eight years, because he was paralyzed.
Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your bed!” Immediately he arose.
All who lived at Lydda and in Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which when translated, means Dorcas. This woman was full of good works and acts of mercy which she did.
In those days, she became sick, and died. When they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
As Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, imploring him not to delay in coming to them.

Peter got up and went with them. When he had come, they brought him into the upper room. All the widows stood by him weeping, and showing the coats and garments which Dorcas had made while she was with them.
Peter sent them all out, and knelt down and prayed. Turning to the body, he said, “Tabitha, get up!” She opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter, she sat up.
He gave her his hand, and raised her up. Calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive.
This became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.
He stayed many days in Joppa with a tanner named Simon.
b: In the last devotion, Saul was sent back to Tarsus and entered a long silence; the churches everywhere had peace, were built up, and multiplied.

Luke moves the camera from Saul back to Peter. During Saul’s silent ten years, God’s work did not stop. This passage records two miracles: a paralytic who had lain eight years rose, and a dead woman disciple came alive. Both resemble things the Lord Jesus did in the Gospels—because the One doing them is still Him.
I. “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you”—The Faucet Is Not the Source of the Water

Verses 32–35: “As Peter went throughout all those parts, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. There he found a certain man named Aeneas, who had been bedridden for eight years, because he was paralyzed. Peter said to him, ‘Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Arise, and make your bed.’ Immediately he arose. All who lived at Lydda and in Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.”

Lydda lies about twenty-five miles northwest of Jerusalem, on the plain of Sharon. Some of the disciples scattered in chapter 8 had settled here, and Luke calls them “saints”—people set apart for God. Peter did not come to hold an evangelistic meeting but to visit these scattered believers. People matter more than tasks; he went first to see people.

There he met Aeneas, paralyzed eight years. Peter’s words deserve to be read word by word: “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you.” Not “I heal you in Jesus’ name,” but “Jesus Christ heals you”—something already done, which Peter simply told him. “Arise, and make your bed”—the Lord Jesus in Capernaum said to the paralytic lowered through the roof, “Arise, take up your bed” (Luke 5:24). Peter did not invent new words; he only repeated the Lord’s.

When a faucet is opened, water comes, yet no one thanks the faucet. It is only the place the water passes through; the source is elsewhere. From the Beautiful Gate in chapter 3 until now, Peter had been doing the same thing: turning people’s eyes from the faucet to the source. “All who lived at Lydda and in Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord”—they turned to the Lord, not to Peter.
• Already healed: Peter only declared what the Lord had done; he was not doing it himself.
• Be the faucet, not the source: let people turn to the Lord, not to me.
II. “Full of good works and acts of mercy”—A Woman Disciple Remembered by Her Deeds

Verses 36–37: “Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which, when translated, means Dorcas. This woman was full of good works and acts of mercy which she did. In those days, she became sick, and died. When they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.”

Joppa is a harbor on the Mediterranean, the very port where Jonah boarded a ship to flee. The word for “woman disciple” appears only here in the whole New Testament—a female “disciple.” Luke uses it deliberately to say: she was not merely a zealous woman; she was a disciple. Tabitha is Aramaic and Dorcas is Greek; both mean “gazelle.”

In introducing her, Luke says nothing of her gifts, status, or preaching; only two things: “full of good works and acts of mercy.” The original means “filled with good deeds and almsgiving.” What was recorded of her life is not what she said but what her hands did. This is exactly what life first looks like: what the life is flows out of the hands. What self-denial looks like in Dorcas: clothing sewn stitch by stitch onto other people.
• She was a “disciple”: following the Lord is not divided by gender, nor by pulpit or needle.
• Remembered by hands: what a person’s life is finally remembered by is what the hands have done.
III. “Please come to us without delay”—The Tunics and Garments of the Widows

Verses 38–39: “As Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, begging him, ‘Please come to us without delay.’ Peter got up and went with them. When he had come, they brought him into the upper room. All the widows stood by him weeping, and showing the coats and garments which Dorcas made while she was with them.”

From Lydda to Joppa is about ten miles, half a day on foot. The disciples sent two men with one sentence: “Come, without delay.” They did not say what they wanted Peter to do—the woman was already dead and laid in the upper room; perhaps they only wanted him to come and mourn together. Peter “got up and went,” without asking why.

The scene upstairs is touching. Widows were the least supported people in that society; they stood weeping, holding the tunics and garments Dorcas had made, “showing” them to him—not displaying keepsakes, but saying: look, this is how she loved us. When a person departs, what the people standing by hold in their hands is a summary of that person’s life. What Dorcas left was not property but love worn on a crowd of people’s bodies.
• Get up and go: go to be with them first; the Lord will make things clear there.
• What I leave in people’s hands: on the day I leave, what will they be holding?
IV. “Tabitha, get up!”—Kneeling, Turning, Reaching Out

Verses 40–42: “But Peter put them all out, and knelt down and prayed. Turning to the body, he said, ‘Tabitha, get up!’ She opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter, she sat up. He gave her his hand, and raised her up. Calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive. And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.”

Every step Peter took he had seen the Lord take. When the Lord raised Jairus’ daughter, He put all the mourners outside (Mark 5:40); Peter also “put them all out.” The Lord said to the little girl “Talitha cumi”; Peter said “Tabitha, get up”—in Aramaic the two sentences differ by one letter. Peter did almost exactly as the Lord had done.

But there is one added action in the middle that the Lord never did: “knelt down and prayed.” The Lord did not need to kneel to raise the dead, for He Himself is life; Peter had to kneel, because he is not. Kneeling is acknowledging: I do not have this power; the power is with Him. This is the eternal difference between every servant and the Lord—He speaks and it is done; we must first kneel. Then he turned, spoke, and reached out his hand to raise her, and “presented her alive.”
• Do as the Lord did, even the gestures: Jesus is an example, not a theory.
• Kneel first: the Lord did not need to kneel; I do, because the power is His, not mine.
V. “He stayed many days in Joppa with one Simon, a tanner”—A Small Step Across the Line
Verse 43: “It happened, that he stayed many days in Joppa with one Simon, a tanner.”

This sentence reads like a footnote but is actually a turning point. A tanner handled the skins of dead animals all day; by Jewish purity rules this was one of the most unclean trades, and ordinary rabbis would not stay in a tanner’s house. Peter stayed—and “many days.”

This was a small step across the line. Peter was not yet prepared to meet Gentiles—that waits until chapter 10, when the Lord told him three times in a vision, “What God has cleansed, don’t you call unclean.” But before that vision, he had already moved into a home that Jews were unwilling to live in. Changing from a human viewpoint to God’s is not done all at once; it comes step by step: a tanner’s house, a vision, a Gentile’s house.
• A turn in the footnote: the Lord’s great work often begins in an unremarkable lodging.
• Take a small step first: before the great vision, move into that house you were unwilling to live in.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Jesus Is My Example, Even to the Gestures
In both miracles of this passage, Peter was “repeating” the Lord.

To Aeneas he spoke the words the Lord had spoken in Capernaum; for Dorcas he did what the Lord had done in Jairus’ house. Peter’s three and a half years beside the Lord were not in vain: he had seen how the Lord did it, and now he did it that way. Jesus is my example—in Acts it is this concrete: not imitating His spirit alone, but learning even the steps and the very words.

Yet Peter had one more action than the Lord: kneeling. The Lord is the source of life; He speaks and it is done. Peter was a faucet; he had to turn first toward the source. Self-denying service is in this “kneeling”—not I can, but He can; not I do, but He has already done it, and I only declare it.
And Dorcas reminds us that a remembered life is not necessarily on the pulpit. Letting Jesus have all the glory can also be sewn stitch by stitch.
a: Be a Faucet
Turn people’s eyes from me to the source; let people turn to the Lord, not to me.
Live Out Life with Your Hands
If my life can only be remembered by what my hands have done, what do I want that to be?
Get Up and Go
When someone says “Come, without delay,” go and be with them first, without asking why.
Kneel First
Before serving, acknowledge I have no power; the power is with Him.
Take a Small Step
Before the great vision comes, move into the house I was unwilling to live in.
q: If you left today, what “tunics and garments” would the people standing by hold in their hands? Are you satisfied with that answer?

Before the vision, Peter first moved into the tanner’s house. Do you have a “tanner’s house” in your life—a place you are unwilling to go because of some squeamishness or prejudice? The Lord may be asking you to take that small step first.
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that during Saul’s silent years Your work did not stop; thank You for letting us see that the Lord Jesus still, through His servants today, raises the paralyzed and the dead. We know the power is not in Peter but in Your Son; Peter was only the one who knelt first.
Lord Jesus, You are our example; we want to be like Peter, learning even Your gestures and Your words. Teach us to be faucets, not the source, and each time someone is helped through us, to turn his eyes to You. Give us the hands of Dorcas, full of good works and acts of mercy, so that our lives flow out from our hands. And lead us to take that small step—to move into the house we were unwilling to live in, so that when Your next vision comes, it may find a person already prepared. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Now there was a certain man in Caesarea, Cornelius by name, a centurion of what was called the Italian Regiment,
a devout man, and one who feared God with all his house, who gave gifts for the needy generously to the people, and always prayed to God.
At about the ninth hour of the day, he clearly saw in a vision an angel of God coming to him, and saying to him, “Cornelius!”
He, fastening his eyes on him, and being frightened, said, “What is it, Lord?” He said to him, “Your prayers and your gifts to the needy have gone up for a memorial before God.
Now send men to Joppa, and get Simon, who is also called Peter.
He is staying with a tanner named Simon, whose house is by the seaside.
When the angel who spoke to him had departed, Cornelius called two of his household servants and a devout soldier of those who waited on him continually.
Having explained everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.
b: 上一篇，彼得在呂大叫癱了八年的以尼雅起來，在約帕叫死了的大比大復活，然後住進了硝皮匠西門的家。硝皮匠整天跟死獸的皮打交道，按猶太人的規矩是不潔淨的行業，虔誠人不會住到他家去。彼得住進去了。神已經悄悄把他放在一條界線的邊上。
現在，鏡頭離開約帕，往北移五十公里，來到一座完全外邦的城。那裡有一個人，也正在禱告。
一、 「在該撒利亞有一個人，名叫哥尼流」——福音走到了帝國的門口
第 1 節一句話，給了三個資料：該撒利亞、義大利營、百夫長。
該撒利亞是大希律建造的海港城，以該撒的名字命名，是羅馬巡撫的駐地——一座從名字到建築都屬於外邦的城。義大利營是由義大利本土人組成的部隊。百夫長帶領約一百名士兵，是從士兵一路打上來的軍官。
所以哥尼流是佔領軍的軍官，是猶太人眼中「他們」的代表。而神揀選的第一個外邦家庭，正是這一家。神的眼光從來不按我們的分類走。我們心裡有多少人，早就被歸到「不可能」那一格？神卻正在那一格裡預備祂的工作。
• 神不按我們的分類：佔領軍的軍官，成了神揀選的第一家。
• 福音要去的地方：往往正是我們劃定「他們」的地方。
二、 「他是個虔誠人……常常禱告神」——很好，但還不夠
第 2 節給哥尼流四個描述：虔誠、全家敬畏神、多多賙濟、常常禱告。
當時猶太人稱這一類人為「敬畏神的人」：外邦人，沒有受割禮，卻厭倦了羅馬的假神，被以色列獨一的神吸引，到會堂聽道、行善事。哥尼流做得比許多猶太人還徹底——不是一個人信，是全家；不是偶爾捐一點，是多多賙濟。
但要留意：這樣一個人，還沒有得救。彼得後來覆述這件事，說天使告訴哥尼流，彼得「有話告訴你，可以叫你和你的全家得救」（徒 11:14）。虔誠、行善、禱告都很好，卻沒有一樣能代替耶穌。哥尼流的好，讓他被神記念；只有耶穌，才讓他得救。
教會裡不缺「好人」，可是好，不等於裡面已經換了生命。舊人有己的生命也可以做很多善事，只是做的時候中心仍然是自己：自己的名聲、自己的安心。新人無己的生命不是做得更多，是中心換成了祂。哥尼流需要的不是再多做一點，是遇見那一位。
• 好人也需要救恩：行善讓神記念，只有耶穌讓人得救。
• 做得多不等於生命改了：中心是自己還是祂，才是分別。
三、 「你的禱告和你的賙濟達到神面前，已蒙記念了」——有人收到了
第 3、4 節，「約在申初」，就是下午三點，聖殿獻晚祭、猶太人固定禱告的時辰（徒 3:1）。一個羅馬軍官，按著猶太人的時辰在自己家裡禱告——他不是隨便信信。
天使叫他的名字，他定睛看，驚怕。天使的第一句話不是命令，是確認：「你的禱告和你的賙濟達到神面前，已蒙記念了。」這是獻祭的用語。舊約的素祭要取一把燒在壇上，「作為紀念」（利 2:2）。天使的意思是：你的禱告和賙濟，像祭物一樣升上去了，神收到了。
我們都寄過那種不知道有沒有人收到的信。寄出時滿心懇切，之後是漫長的沉默，久了連自己都懷疑那封信是不是丟了。哥尼流禱告了很久，從來沒有人告訴他有沒有到達。直到這一天，神差人來說：收到了，一件也沒有漏。
這是給每一個長久禱告卻沒有回音的人的話。你的禱告沒有掉在半路上。神不是不記得，祂是在預備一個比你所求更大的答覆——哥尼流求的大概只是更認識神，神給他的是全家得救，並且叫他成為福音進入外邦的第一道門。
• 禱告是升上去的祭：沒有一句掉在半路。
• 神的答覆常常比所求更大：他求認識，神給救恩。
四、 「你當打發人往約帕去，請那稱呼彼得的西門來」——天使不傳福音，人傳
第 5、6 節有一件奇怪的事。天使已經站在哥尼流面前了，為什麼不直接把福音講給他聽？
天使只給了一個地址：約帕，海邊，硝皮匠西門的家。地址精確到門牌，內容卻一個字都沒有。神定意要人從人聽見福音。
第一，傳福音的職分神託付給了人，不給天使。第二，神要的不只是哥尼流得救，還要彼得被改變。天使若直接講了，彼得就還坐在自己的圍牆裡。第三，人比事重要，關係比東西重要——神不是要送一份「資訊」給哥尼流，祂要的是一個外邦軍官與一個猶太漁夫坐在同一個屋簷下，成為一家人。
還要留意那個地址：硝皮匠西門的家。神在約帕早就把彼得往界線上推了一步，好叫該撒利亞來的人來敲門的時候，敲得到。神總是同時在兩頭作工。
• 福音是人傳的：天使有地址，沒有信息；信息在人身上。
• 兩頭都被改變：哥尼流要得救，彼得要打開。
五、 「把這事都述說給他們聽，就打發他們往約帕去」——立刻，不等明天
第 7、8 節，天使走後，哥尼流叫了兩個家人和一個「虔誠兵」。他的信仰不是關起門來的私事，連身邊的兵都跟著信。
他做了兩件事。第一，「把這事都述說給他們聽」，不隱瞞、不打折。第二，「就打發他們往約帕去」。他自己後來說：「我立時打發人去請你」（徒 10:33）。申初領受，天使一走，人就上路。
順服最大的敵人不是拒絕，是「等一下」。等我想清楚、等狀況更適合。哥尼流不知道彼得是誰、肯不肯來、來了會說什麼；他知道的只有一件——神說了，就去。這就是聖靈是我的引導最平常的樣子：不是等所有問題都有答案才動，是在只知道下一步的時候，就走那一步。
• 述說出來：領受的不藏在心裡，讓身邊的人一起有分。
• 立時打發：順服不看時機成熟，看的是主說了沒有。
321 理念亮光：神在兩頭作工，我只要在我這一頭順服
這八節是一個更大故事的開頭。故事的兩頭，一頭在該撒利亞，一頭在約帕；一頭是外邦軍官在申初禱告，一頭是猶太使徒明天要在午正禱告。兩個人彼此不認識，神卻同時對兩個人說話。
我們常常想看見全局才肯動。可是哥尼流只有一個地址。神沒有把全局給他，只把下一步給他；他做了那一步，神就把另一頭接上了。
有己的生命要掌握全局，因為它信不過那位掌管全局的；它要把每一種可能都想過才敢動——這就是用腦靠自己，愈想愈煩惱。無己的生命只做自己這一頭的事：禱告、行善、聽見了就去。至於另一頭——彼得肯不肯來——那是神的事。讓神作神，讓人作人；人的本位不是掌管全局，是順服眼前這一步。焦點在耶穌，不在自己、不在別人、不在環境。這樣的人，神就用他打開一整個世界的門。
a: 拆掉自己的分類
你心裡歸入「不可能」的那些人，正是神在預備的地方。
分清好與得救
虔誠、行善都很好，但只有耶穌能救；不要把好當作已經得救。
相信禱告已上達
長久沒有回音的禱告，沒有一句掉在半路。
做人該做的那一頭
福音是人傳的，別等天使代替你去。
立時，不等一下
主已經說了的事，今天就走那一步。
q: 你心裡有沒有一個人或一群人，是你已經默默歸入「福音不可能臨到」那一格的？如果神正在那一格裡預備祂的工作，祂會要你先做哪一步？
哥尼流「立時」打發人去。你現在有沒有一件已經清楚是主要你做的事，卻還停在「等一下」？攔住你的，是缺少答案，還是缺少順服？
pr:
親愛的天父，謝謝祢，祢的眼目看見該撒利亞的一個軍官，看見一個在我們眼中屬於「他們」的人，並且記念他每一次的禱告與賙濟。謝謝祢讓我們知道，我們向祢所獻上的，沒有一件掉在半路上，祢都收到了，並且祢的答覆比我們所求的更大。
主耶穌，我們承認，我們常常把人分類，把福音的門關在自己畫的線裡面；也承認我們順服的時候總想先看見全局，總說「等一下」。求祢赦免我們。求祢把哥尼流的心賜給我們——聽見了就述說，領受了就打發，不知道另一頭會怎樣也照樣上路。求聖靈作我們的引導，叫我們不用腦靠自己想遍所有的可能，只用心靠祢走眼前的一步。也求祢提醒我們，好不等於得救，虔誠不能代替祢；願我們所做的一切，中心都是祢，不是我們自己。奉主耶穌基督的名禱告，阿們。

v: Now on the next day as they were on their journey, and got close to the city, Peter went up on the housetop to pray at about noon.
He became hungry and desired to eat, but while they were preparing, he fell into a trance.
He saw heaven opened and a certain container descending to him, like a great sheet let down by four corners on the earth,
in which were all kinds of four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, reptiles, and birds of the sky.
A voice came to him, “Rise, Peter, kill and eat!”
But Peter said, “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.”
A voice came to him again the second time, “What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean.”
This was done three times, and immediately the vessel was received up into heaven.
b: 上一篇，哥尼流在申初領受了異象，天使一走，三個人就上路，往約帕去了。神在該撒利亞那一頭動了工。
這一篇，鏡頭切回約帕。「第二天，他們行路將近那城」——就在三個人快要走到的時候，海邊的一間屋子上，彼得正上了房頂禱告。神在兩頭作工，時間對得分毫不差。哥尼流那一頭需要的是順服，彼得這一頭需要的卻是：被拆掉一道牆。
一、 「彼得約在午正，上房頂去禱告」——神在人禱告的時候說話
第 9 節，「約在午正」，就是中午十二點。猶太人固定的禱告時辰是早晨、申初和傍晚，午正不在其中。彼得是額外去禱告的——沒有人規定，他自己上去。
當時的房子是平頂，房頂是家裡最安靜的地方。中午太陽正烈，一個人上到頂上，遠離底下的忙碌，單獨面對神。使徒行傳裡最重要的幾個轉折，都發生在有人禱告的時候：五旬節前是禱告，揀選馬提亞前是禱告，如今福音要跨出猶太人的界線，兩頭的人也都在禱告。
神不是只在禱告的時候才說話，但人往往只在禱告的時候才聽得見。三個人走近城門的那一刻，若彼得在底下忙著，這個異象就沒有地方落下來。關係的次序是先與神、再與自己、再與人、再與事——彼得先上了房頂，神才把該撒利亞的事接到他身上。
• 額外的禱告：不是規定的時辰，是自己上去的；神常在這樣的時刻說話。
• 先上房頂：先與神，神才把人與事接過來。
二、 「覺得餓了……魂遊象外」——神用他的餓來教他
第 10 到 12 節，彼得禱告的時候餓了，底下正在做飯。就在這個最日常的處境裡，他「魂遊象外」——不是睡著作夢，是清醒中被帶進一個異象。
天開了，一塊大布繫著四角縋下來，裡面「有地上各樣四足的走獸和昆蟲，並天上的飛鳥」。這個清單不是隨便列的。利未記十一章把動物分成潔淨與不潔淨兩類：分蹄倒嚼的走獸可以吃，其餘不可；昆蟲大多不可；許多飛鳥不可。這是猶太人從小背到大的規矩，是他們與外邦人分別出來的記號之一。如今一塊布上，潔淨的與不潔淨的混在一起，全部縋到他面前。
神用了彼得的餓來作教材，在他餓的時候，把一桌他不肯吃的東西擺在他眼前。神最常用的教室，不是特別的聚會，是我們最日常的需要——餓了、累了、缺了的時候。
• 最日常的教室：神用一頓飯的時間，講一件改變歷史的事。
• 混在一起的布：神故意把彼得分開的東西放在一起。
三、 「主啊，這是不可的」——認祂為主，卻對祂說「不可」
第 13、14 節，聲音說：「彼得，起來，宰了吃！」彼得回答：「主啊，這是不可的！凡俗物和不潔淨的物，我從來沒有吃過。」
這一句話裡有一個矛盾。他叫祂「主」，卻對祂說「不可」。既然是主，哪有「不可」？可是彼得就是這樣回答的——而且理由是「我從來沒有」。
要體諒彼得。他一生守這規矩，這不是頑固，是敬虔。更叫人深思的是，主耶穌早就講過「各樣的食物都是潔淨的」（可 7:19），那一次彼得就在場。話他聽過了，卻沒有聽進去，因為那和他從小的習慣不合。
開車的人都有經驗：導航說「前方請右轉」，可是我們每天走的是左轉，手就自然往左打了，還覺得導航錯了。彼得的「不可」就是這樣——不是他不愛主，是他的手已經習慣了往左。有己的生命最深的藏身處，不是明顯的罪，是多年的敬虔習慣。它披著「我從來沒有」的外衣，讓我們對主說不的時候，還以為自己在守規矩。
• 主與不可不能並存：叫祂主，就沒有「不可」的餘地。
• 己藏在習慣裡：「我從來沒有」，常常是己最虔誠的一句話。
四、 「神所潔淨的，你不可當作俗物」——潔淨的主權在神
第 15 節，第二次的聲音只有一句：「神所潔淨的，你不可當作俗物。」
「俗物」在原文是「共通的、平常的」——猶太人用來指混雜在外邦人中間、沒有分別出來的東西。「潔淨」則是一個已經完成的動作：神已經潔淨了，不是「你可以看作潔淨」。彼得的問題不在於他有標準，在於他的標準停在神已經往前走的那一點之後。
這句話的重點不是食物。到了第 28 節彼得自己就解開了：「神已經指示我，無論甚麼人都不可看作俗而不潔淨的。」布上的動物是課本，課本裡的內容是人。神要拆的，是彼得心裡那道把人分成「我們」與「他們」的牆。
聖經是我的準則——這句話彼得會完全同意。但準則是神的話，不是我從神的話裡養成的傳統。當傳統和神現在的話衝突，人就要選一邊。從人的觀點改成神的觀點，地上的改成天上的：這是彼得此刻站在房頂上要做的一個改變。
• 潔淨是神做的：不是我判定誰潔淨，是我承認祂已經潔淨了誰。
• 動物是課本，人是內容：神拆的是牆，不是餐桌的規矩。
五、 「這樣一連三次」——三次，還是那個彼得；三次，還是那位主
第 16 節，「這樣一連三次，那物隨即收回天上去了。」
彼得的一生和「三次」分不開：炭火旁三次不認主，海邊三次被問「你愛我嗎」，如今房頂上三次聽見「起來，宰了吃」。他還是那個彼得——衝口而出、先說不可、要主重複三遍才慢慢轉過來。但祂也還是那位主——不放棄、不動怒，一次不夠就第二次、第三次。
還要留意一件事：布收回去了，但神沒有給解釋。彼得帶著滿肚子的疑問下了房頂（第 17 節說他「心裡正在猜疑之間」）。神並不總是在異象裡把答案講完，祂常常把答案放在下一步——就是那三個正在敲門的人身上。彼得不需要在房頂上想通，他只需要下去開門。
• 三次的耐心：我們慢，主不急；祂一遍一遍地說。
• 答案在門口：異象裡沒講完的，神放在下一步的順服裡。
321 理念亮光：改變觀念就改變生命
哥尼流那一頭，神要的是順服；彼得這一頭，神要的是改變觀念。兩樣都不容易，但改變觀念更難——因為要改的不是一件錯事，是一件他一生以為對的事。
改變觀念就改變生命，改變生命就改變生活；改變從我開始。彼得若不在房頂上先被改變，下去見那三個人的時候，就會照著老規矩把他們擋在門外。整個世界的門，繫在一個人肯不肯讓神更正他的觀念上。
有己的生命護著自己的觀念，因為觀念是它多年建起來的家；神說「起來，宰了吃」，它的第一反應是「不可」。無己的生命也有觀念、也有原則，但它把最後的裁決權交在神手裡——祂說潔淨的，我就不再說俗。謙卑不是沒有立場，是立場之上還有一位主；謙卑在今天看得見的樣子，就是當神藉著祂的話、藉著弟兄姊妹更正我的時候，我不先說「我從來沒有」，而是先問「主，祢要我看見什麼」。
a: 上房頂
在規定的時辰以外，給神一段額外的安靜，祂常在那裡說話。
在餓的時候聽
神用最日常的需要作教室，不要錯過。
檢查「不可」
你對主說過的「不可」，理由是不是「我從來沒有」？
承認祂已潔淨
不是我判定誰乾淨，是承認神已經接納了誰。
帶著問題下樓
不必想通才動，答案常在下一步的順服裡。
q: 想一件你多年來一直以為「當然如此」的信仰習慣或做法。你有沒有問過主，那是祂的準則，還是你從祂的準則養成的傳統？
神叫彼得帶著疑問下樓去開門。你此刻有沒有一件還沒想通、卻已經知道下一步是什麼的事？你願意先走那一步嗎？
pr:
親愛的天父，謝謝祢，祢在兩頭同時作工，時間分毫不差；祢用一頓飯的時間、一個人的餓，講一件要改變整個世界的事。謝謝祢對彼得的耐心，一次、兩次、三次，不放棄，也不動怒。
主耶穌，我們承認，我們也常常一面叫祢主，一面對祢說不可；我們最不肯讓祢碰的，往往不是明顯的罪，是多年的習慣、一生以為對的觀念。求祢赦免我們把自己的傳統當作祢的準則。求祢像對彼得一樣，把我們分開的東西放在一起，讓我們看見祢已經潔淨了誰、接納了誰。求聖靈更正我們的觀念，叫我們的生命被改變，生活跟著改變；也叫我們願意帶著還沒想通的問題，就先下樓去開門。願祢在我們的觀念上作王，得著一切的榮耀。奉主耶穌基督的名禱告，阿們。

v: Now while Peter was very perplexed in himself what the vision which he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood before the gate,
and called and asked whether Simon, who was also called Peter, was lodging there.
While Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three  men seek you.
But arise, get down, and go with them, doubting nothing; for I have sent them.”
Peter went down to the men, and said, “Behold, I am he whom you seek. Why have you come?”

They said, “Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous man and one who fears God, and well spoken of by all the nation of the Jews, was directed by a holy angel to invite you to his house, and to listen to what you say.”
So he called them in and provided a place to stay. On the next day Peter arose and went out with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.
b: 上一篇，布收回天上去了，神卻沒有給彼得解釋。他站在房頂上，滿心疑問。
這一篇，答案來了——不是從天上，是從門外。就在他還在想那異象是什麼意思的時候，樓下有人喊他的名字。神把兩頭的線在這一刻接上了。
一、 「彼得心裡正在猜疑之間……站在門外」——答案不在房頂上，在門口
第 17、18 節，路加用了一個很精準的並排：彼得在樓上「猜疑」，三個人在樓下「站在門外」。
「猜疑」不是懷疑神，是想不通。他一生守的規矩被神翻了三次，他不知道這是什麼意思。就在他想的時候，哥尼流差來的人「訪問到西門的家」——一路打聽，找到了海邊這間硝皮匠的屋子——「喊著問：有稱呼彼得的西門住在這裡沒有？」
拼圖的人都知道，手上一片拼不上去的時候，不是那一片有問題，是另一片還沒到。彼得手上有一片：布、動物、「神所潔淨的」。這一片單獨看，怎麼看都不通。另一片正在門口喊他的名字。神常常這樣帶領——先給一片看不懂的，再給另一片，兩片合起來才成圖。想不通的時候，不必硬想，聽一聽門口有沒有聲音。
• 猜疑不是不信：想不通是正常的，神的圖還沒拼完。
• 另一片在門口：想不通的異象，常常由一個人的敲門聲來解開。
二、 「聖靈向他說……不要疑惑，因為是我差他們來的」——聖靈引導的樣子
第 19、20 節，彼得還在思想，「聖靈向他說：有三個人來找你。起來，下去，和他們同往，不要疑惑，因為是我差他們來的。」
留意這段話的樣子。聖靈沒有解釋異象，祂只給了四個動作：起來、下去、同往、不要疑惑。動作很清楚，理由只有一句：「是我差他們來的。」
「不要疑惑」這個詞，原文也可以譯作「不要分別等類」（見徒 11:12 小字）。這正是全段的關鍵——聖靈對彼得說的不只是「別懷疑」，更是「別把人分類」。不要看他們是外邦人、是羅馬兵，就把他們歸到另一類去。
還有一句更妙：「是我差他們來的。」明明是哥尼流差的，聖靈卻說是我差的。當神在動工，人手所做的一切，背後都是祂。這就是聖靈是我的引導在生活中的樣子：祂很少把整幅圖解釋給我們看，祂通常只說下一步——起來，下去，跟他們走。至於為什麼，走了才知道。用心靠聖靈，就是聽見「下去」就下去；用腦靠自己，就是站在樓上把理由想完才肯動，結果門口的人早就走了。
• 聖靈給動作，不給全圖：起來、下去、同往——先走，再懂。
• 不要分別等類：門口的人不是「那一類」，是祂差來的。
三、 「我就是你們所找的人。你們來是為甚麼緣故」——先下去，再問
第 21 節，彼得下去了。他說了兩句話：「我就是你們所找的人。你們來是為甚麼緣故？」
第一句是承認：我就是。他沒有躲、沒有叫硝皮匠出去打發他們、沒有先問清楚再決定要不要露面。第二句是發問：你們為什麼來？他沒有預設答案，讓對方說。
這兩句話看起來平常，卻是一個剛被翻轉的人才說得出來的。若是一小時前的彼得——那個說「主啊，這是不可的」的彼得——他大概會站在樓上先問明白。現在他下去了，站在三個外邦人面前，先把自己交出去，再聽對方要什麼。
我們常常倒過來：先問清楚對方是誰、要什麼，再決定要不要下去。可是人比事重要，關係比東西重要。彼得先站到人面前，事情才有得談。順服的第一步，往往是身體先動——下樓，開門，站到那個人面前。
• 先露面：我就是；不躲在樓上把人打發掉。
• 先問，不預設：你們為什麼來？讓對方說，不替對方決定。
四、 「百夫長哥尼流是個義人，敬畏神，為猶太通國所稱讚」——神早已在對方身上動工
第 22 節，三個人開口了：「百夫長哥尼流是個義人，敬畏神，為猶太通國所稱讚。他蒙一位聖天使指示，叫他請你到他家裡去，聽你的話。」
他們知道彼得是猶太人，所以特別說明：哥尼流「為猶太通國所稱讚」——他不是敵人，連猶太人都說他好。他們也把來意說得極清楚：不是請彼得去做什麼，是去「聽你的話」。哥尼流要的不是神蹟、不是幫助，是話。
彼得聽到這裡，房頂上的那片拼圖就對上了。神已經在該撒利亞預備了一個人、一個家、一群等著聽的人。彼得不是去開荒，是去收割神早已預備的。我們往往以為傳福音是「我去把神帶給他」；其實更多時候，是神早已在那裡等著，只叫我們去把祂已經做的事說出來。焦點在耶穌，不在自己——不是我多會講，是祂早已在那裡。
• 對方早被預備：神先在哥尼流身上動工，才差彼得去。
• 去說，不是去造：不是把神帶去，是把祂已經做的事講出來。
五、 「彼得就請他們進去，住了一宿……還有約帕的幾個弟兄同著他去」——第一步跨線，在自己家門口
第 23 節有兩個動作，都很不起眼，卻都很重要。
第一，「彼得就請他們進去，住了一宿」。三個外邦人，其中一個是羅馬兵，被請進了一個猶太人的家過夜。按當時的規矩，猶太人不可與外邦人親近來往（第 28 節）。福音跨進外邦，第一步不是在該撒利亞，是在約帕——在彼得自己住的地方，從請人進門開始。跨線從來不是先去很遠的地方，是先在自己家門口打開門。
第二，「還有約帕的幾個弟兄同著他去」。後來我們知道是六位（徒 11:12）。彼得知道這件事會有爭議，所以他不獨行。一方面是見證——回耶路撒冷的時候，有六個人可以作證；另一方面，這是無己的謙卑——他不把這件破天荒的事攬在自己一個人身上。謙卑在這裡看得見的樣子，就是：做一件大事之前，先找幾個弟兄同去，讓自己不是唯一能說話的人。
• 從家門口開始：跨線的第一步，是請門口的人進來住一宿。
• 不獨行：帶弟兄同去，讓見證不只在我一個人身上。
321 理念亮光：無己才能被聖靈引導
這七節裡，聖靈說話只有一次，說的是：起來，下去，同往，不要疑惑。
聖靈的引導很少長篇大論，通常就是這麼幾個字。難的不在於聽不見，難的在於聽見了肯不肯動。彼得能被引導，不是因為他特別屬靈，是因為他在房頂上已經被拆了一道牆——「我從來沒有」那句話被打斷了三次，他的己鬆了。己一鬆，聖靈一句「下去」他就下去了。
有己的生命也想被引導，但它要先看到理由、先確認結果、先分好等類。這樣的人，聖靈的話會一直卡在「為什麼」上面過不去。無己的生命不是沒有問題，彼得也「猜疑」；但它把問題帶著，先走那一步——下樓、開門、請人進來、明天同去。無己不再是我，乃是基督；引導就不再是我聽了再評估，而是祂說了我就走。這樣的人，神能用他把一整個世界的門打開。
a: 別硬想，聽門口
想不通的異象，答案常由一個人的敲門聲來解開。
聽見就下去
聖靈給的是動作，不是全圖；先走，再懂。
不要分別等類
門口的那個人，不是「那一類」，是祂差來的。
先露面再問
站到人面前，讓對方說，不替對方決定。
從家門口跨線
請人進來住一宿，比去遠方更難，也更真。
q: 你現在有沒有一個想不通的處境，其實神的另一片拼圖已經在「門口」——某一個人、某一件事——只是你還在樓上硬想？
「不要分別等類。」你心裡有沒有一類人，是聖靈叫你去、你卻先把他們歸類的？今天跨線的第一步，可以是在你自己的家門口做什麼？
pr:
親愛的天父，謝謝祢，彼得在房頂上想不通的時候，祢已經把答案帶到門口。謝謝祢在該撒利亞早已預備了一個人、一個家、一群等著聽道的人；我們所去的每一個地方，祢都先到了。
主耶穌，我們承認，我們常常站在樓上把理由想完才肯下去，門口的人早已走了；我們也常常先把人分了等類，才決定要不要開門。求祢赦免我們。求聖靈也向我們說「起來，下去，同往，不要疑惑」，並且賜我們一顆鬆開的心，聽見了就走。求祢叫我們從自己的家門口開始跨線——請進門、住一宿、一同上路；也叫我們不獨行，凡事帶著弟兄，不把祢的工作攬在自己身上。願祢作我們的引導，也得著一切的榮耀。奉主耶穌基督的名禱告，阿們。

v: On the next day they entered into Caesarea. Cornelius was waiting for them, having called together his relatives and his near friends.
When Peter entered, Cornelius met him, fell down at his feet, and worshiped him.
But Peter raised him up, saying, “Stand up! I myself am also a man.”
As he talked with him, he went in and found many gathered together.

He said to them, “You yourselves know how it is an unlawful thing for a man who is a Jew to join himself or come to one of another nation, but God has shown me that I shouldn’t call any man unholy or unclean.
Therefore I also came without complaint when I was sent for. I ask therefore, why did you send for me?”
Cornelius said, “Four days ago, I was fasting until this hour, and at the ninth hour, I prayed in my house, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing,
and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer is heard, and your gifts to the needy are remembered in the sight of God.
Send therefore to Joppa, and summon Simon, who is also called Peter. He is staying in the house of a tanner named Simon, by the seaside. When he comes, he will speak to you.’
Therefore I sent to you at once, and it was good of you to come. Now therefore we are all here present in the sight of God to hear all things that have been commanded you by God.”
b: 上一篇，彼得請三個外邦人進門住了一宿，次日帶著約帕的幾個弟兄上路。福音跨出猶太人的界線，第一步已經在他自己家門口踏出去了。
這一篇，兩頭的人終於見面。一個羅馬軍官和一個猶太漁夫，在該撒利亞的一間屋子裡站到了一起。兩個人都被神預備過，兩個人也都要在這場相遇裡再被修正一次。
一、 「哥尼流已經請了他的親屬密友等候他們」——把家打開，把人叫齊
第 24 節，「又次日，他們進入該撒利亞」。從約帕出發走了一天多，到了。哥尼流不是一個人在等，「已經請了他的親屬密友等候他們」。
他派人去請一個素未謀面的猶太人，不知道對方肯不肯來、來了會說什麼，卻不等確定，就先把親戚朋友都叫齊了。第 27 節說「有好些人在那裡聚集」。哥尼流的信心不是「等我先聽聽看，好的話再介紹給別人」，是「神說了有話要給我，那就叫所有我在乎的人一起來聽」。
一個人得了好東西，最自然的反應是先藏好；一個人得了神的話，最自然的反應應該是把家打開。哥尼流的家從第 2 節就是全家敬畏神的家，如今更成了福音第一次進入外邦的家。屬神的體系不是從組織架構開始的，是從一個人肯把家門打開開始的。
• 不等確定就邀人：神說有話要給我，就叫我在乎的人一起來聽。
• 家是第一個領域：屬神的體系，常常從一間打開的屋子開始。
二、 「你起來，我也是人」——不接受不屬於自己的榮耀
第 25、26 節，彼得一進門，哥尼流「就迎接他，俯伏在他腳前拜他」。彼得「卻拉他，說：你起來，我也是人。」
哥尼流是百夫長，在該撒利亞是有身分的人。他俯伏在一個猶太漁夫腳前，是極大的敬意——在他的觀念裡，天使指示要請的人，必定超乎常人。可是彼得立刻把他拉起來。「我也是人」，原文是「我自己也不過是一個人」。
郵差把一封重要的信送到，收信人激動得向郵差下拜。郵差會怎麼做？他會說：我只是送信的，信不是我寫的。彼得正是這樣。他帶來的話是主的，他自己只是送話的人。哥尼流拜錯了對象，彼得若接受了，整場相遇的焦點就從耶穌移到了彼得身上。
